title: MetaScience, Scientific Inquiry, and Agents

About this Group Meeting
Drafted v0.5 · public book narrowed to what the group has covered · October 20, 2026
MetaScience, Scientific Inquiry, and Agents · Denolle Lab · meetings taken one at a time

title: MetaScience, Scientific Inquiry, and Agents
text:
What this book is for

Define the modes of inquiry as the literature invokes and uses them: observation, exploration, hypothesis assessment, theory, simulation, instruments, methods, synthesis, robustness, estimation, regularities.
Define the outcomes we want to maximize: scientific advance, impact, novelty, and breadth or polymathy, with how each has been measured and where the measures fail.
Build a general graph of inquiry progressively, one reading at a time, and test it on successful and ordinary papers: where each paper enters, which steps it takes, where it ends, and how it scores.
Each mode will become a specialist agent. The definitions and tests here are what those agents’ rubrics start from.

title: MetaScience, Scientific Inquiry, and Agents

How we meet

One anchor reading for everyone, one companion presented by a rotating reader; optional readings are resources.
Each meeting leaves one ledger row and three sentences: what changed, what evidence warrants it, what follows for the agents or their evaluation.
Distinguish a primary result, a philosophical argument, a historical reconstruction, an empirical association, and a benchmark.

crumbs: Scientific advance and modes of inquiry

title: Scientific advance and modes of inquiry
text:
Scientific advance is the primary outcome: a warranted gain in knowledge, understanding, or research capability relative to a stated starting point.
Human-defined epistemic modes organize how an agent pursues that gain; novelty, correctness/warrant, and impact help assess it.
These overlapping profiles are proposals for geosciences. They draw on philosophy, history, and empirical studies of scientific process and impact (Hacking 1992; Fortunato et al. 2018).
Hacking’s discussion of styles supplies historical/philosophical context, not validation of this vocabulary. Our modes are not the science-policy distinction called Mode 1/Mode 2.
The reasoning vocabulary the profiles assume, deduction, induction, abduction, and the verbs test, confirm, exclude, and corroborate, is defined once on the unit of inquiry, with the graph every episode is placed on.
Keep purpose, actions, and context linked: a mode states the epistemic purpose and evidence standards; actions implement it; context records contributions, users, infrastructure, and constraints.
Multiple modes may describe one episode. Do not force a decisive mode for a whole paper; allow unknown, insufficient record, and work outside the current vocabulary.

title: Scientific advance and modes of inquiry
text:
Working mode specifications

Each linked page is the authoritative version for teaching and agent-instruction export. Its actions and transitions are design hypotheses.
What a mode is, the sources that define each profile, how they sit on graph v0.4, and the evidence on novelty, breadth, and advance: Modes of inquiry. The nearest precedent for the word is O’Malley and colleagues’ four modes of research practice; moving between modes is methodological iteration (Elliott 2012).
Thirteen profiles (October 21, 2026): the earlier eleven, with synthesis split into cross-study synthesis and reconstruction from traces, and question-driven inquiry added. The count is provisional.




Profile
Scientific gain it can support
Main nodes on graph v0.4




Question-driven inquiry
A question posed or reframed so that some result would answer it, with presupposition, contrast class, and constraints stated.
Q (and the return from question 8 of the tree)


Observation and description
A credible phenomenon, distribution, baseline, or consequential coverage limit.
O, E


Exploratory inquiry
A developed phenomenon, representation, question, or credible candidate for follow-up.
E


Hypothesis assessment
Discrimination among alternatives; rival generation is a separate action from testing.
H, D, X, P, R


Theory and mechanistic modeling
A concept, explanation, or valid derivation that changes what can be understood or tested.
H, S


Simulation and prediction
Assessed forecasts or useful conditional model consequences.
S


Instruments and observing systems
A reliable new measurement capability.
N


Methods and computation
A new inference or computational capability.
N, I


Cross-study synthesis
A pooled estimate or a connection across studies that no single study supports.
O, C, and K across studies (a composition)


Reconstruction from traces
A constrained history of a past event, retained against rival histories.
F found, O over independent traces, K (the trace-series composition)


Replication and robustness assessment
A corrected result, supported range, or meaningful independent corroboration.
V


Inferential estimation
A latent quantity with uncertainty, resolution, and identified limits.
I


Statistical modeling and empirical regularities
An informative relation or distribution with a warranted range of application.
C and K across repetitions (a composition)

title: Scientific advance and modes of inquiry
text:
Coding an episode

Record the question before/after, actions and artifacts, modes, evidence basis, and next decision in the ledger.
Keep contribution types separate: new data, estimate, instrument, method, concept, synthesis, or replication; enabling/corrective/integrative are roles, not importance ranks.
Record understanding/use aims, co-production, infrastructure, constraints, question origin, and later reframing. Usefulness and legitimacy require their own evidence (Stokes 1997; Cash et al. 2003).
A tomography episode estimates a structure using inversion and sensitivity analysis; a later episode uses it to assess tectonic explanations. The resulting image is inferred, not a direct observation.
A derivation can follow observations and be mathematically valid before any new measurement. Empirical adequacy is a further claim.
A fitted seismic relation can be descriptive, predictive, and mechanistic in different respects. Breiman’s cultures and Shmueli’s objectives are different lenses (Breiman 2001; Shmueli 2010).
crumbs: Scientific advance and modes of inquiry

title: Scientific advance and modes of inquiry
text:
Terms of assessment

Scientific advance

A meaningful, evidenced before/after improvement in what can be known, explained, predicted, measured, or investigated; knowledge and understanding accounts are open to discussion (Bird 2007; Dellsén 2016).
State the frame: task/project, historical knowledge at a date, or contemporary field. Reproducing an old discovery can demonstrate task competence without a new field advance.
Primary evaluation: the fraction of held-out cases achieving a prespecified meaningful warranted gain, with magnitude, failures, uncertainty, and case-family results. The rubric specifies its limits.
Neither a fixed novelty × correctness × impact formula nor contribution count defines advance.



Research question

The seminar’s definition (synthesis, October 21, 2026): an interrogative that states what it presupposes, which alternatives count as answers (its contrast class), and the constraints a satisfactory answer must meet, so that one can say before the work which outcomes would answer it, a contradiction included. Sources: Fraassen (1980); Nickles (1981); Hintikka (1981); Klahr and Simon (1999); Richardson et al. (1995); Love (2008).
Narrower than a programmatic question. “What is an earthquake?” (National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine 2020, 19) is a problem agenda: it has no contrast class or answer criterion, and a project question has to be derived from it.
Wider than a hypothesis. A hypothesis is one candidate answer put up for test (Glass 2010).
Wider than a research idea. In the AI ideation literature an idea already contains a candidate answer and a test (problem, method, experiment plan) (Si et al. 2025; Baek et al. 2025; Wang et al. 2024). An idea comes after a question.
The mode that poses and reframes questions: question-driven inquiry.



Success and failure of a project

Success (convenor, October 21, 2026): a conclusion is reached. A claim is kept with its status, a rival is excluded, or a claim is contradicted. A contradicted claim is a successful result.
Failure: no conclusion is reached after the question has been reframed (decision tree, question 8). A powered null result is a conclusion, not a failure.
These describe a project. Scientific advance, novelty, impact, and breadth describe what a conclusion contributes; they are scored separately.



Idea

The unit that novelty and uptake are assigned to. The readings use four different units, and a novelty score is only comparable with another computed on the same unit.




Unit
Definition in the source
Source




A research idea
A sufficiently specified research project that proposes a motivated method and a practical way to test it, not a short concept or hypothesis alone
Si et al. (2025), as summarized in the meeting 10 notes


A link between two concepts
Two concepts from a topic model put together in one document for the first time in the corpus
Hofstra et al. (2020)


A combination of prior work
A pair of journals co-cited in one reference list
Uzzi et al. (2013); Wang et al. (2017)


A contribution or claim
An observation, method, concept, explanation, connection, or question, stated atomically
Novelty Dossier




On the unit graph, an idea in Si’s sense is a pass through Q, H, S, and D without F, O, or C: a question, a hypothesis, and a designed test, not yet run. A link in Hofstra’s sense is part of what happens at H, generation by joining two concepts.



Novelty

Newness of a specific contribution relative to a stated corpus and date (Uzzi et al. 2013; Fontana et al. 2020).
Record closest precedent, new component, search coverage, and uncertainty; semantic or citation distance is a proxy (Shibayama et al. 2021).
Say “no precedent located within this search.” Distinguish discovery data from later evaluation data. Novelty Dossier.
The same word names different constructs. Meeting 10 read three of them side by side:










Construct
What is new
How it is judged
Source




Atypical combination
A pair of cited journals that co-occurs less often than in a randomized citation network; atypical pairs are those in the 10th percentile of z-scores
Computed; no human in the loop
Uzzi et al. (2013)


First-ever combination
A journal pair cited together for the first time, weighted by how difficult the pairing is
Computed
Wang et al. (2017)


New conceptual link
A concept pair never linked before in the corpus; counted per thesis
Computed from a topic model
Hofstra et al. (2020)


Semantic distance
Distance between cited works, or between concepts, in an embedding space
Computed; validated against authors’ own ratings in one field
Shibayama et al. (2021)


Rated difference from prior art
“Whether the idea is creative and different from existing works on the topic, and brings fresh insights,” with all work online before a stated cutoff treated as prior
1 to 10 expert rating against written anchors
Si et al. (2025)


Originality as a review criterion
One of four dimensions a funder’s panel scores
Expert panel; compared with a language model’s ranking
Machado (2026)




Two rules follow for this group’s records. State the construct with the score: “novel” without its unit and its judge is not a finding. And state the cutoff date: Si’s reviewers used July 2024; a computed measure uses the corpus it was run on.
Si’s rubric bundles two things, difference from prior work and “fresh insights.” An idea can be unprecedented and useless. The Dossier keeps them apart: difference goes in “new component,” usefulness in the advance profile.



Proximal and distal novelty

Proximal novelty links two concepts inside one cluster of a field’s vocabulary. Distal novelty bridges two clusters. Distance is the embedding distance between the linked concepts, averaged per document (Hofstra et al. 2020).
Distal novelty is the continuous form of what the combination measures call atypicality and what the breadth literature calls interdisciplinarity. Fontana’s point applies: a distance score may be measuring interdisciplinarity rather than newness (Fontana et al. 2020).
In Hofstra’s data, uptake falls steeply with distance: distal links are “difficult to integrate into localized conversations within prevailing fields” (Hofstra et al. 2020). Distal novelty is the kind least likely to travel, not the kind least likely to matter.



Correctness and evidential warrant

Assess mathematical/empirical adequacy separately from what the available evidence justified at the time.
The mode specifies relevant evidence: validity of a derivation, calibrated uncertainty, independent observations, discriminating consequences, or sensitivity to assumptions.
A completed checklist cannot guarantee truth. Record supported scope, unknowns, contradictions, and dated later reassessment (Oreskes et al. 1994; Flake and Fried 2020).
No contradiction found, continued citation, and reproducible code are not sufficient evidence of correctness.



Impact

Observed downstream use or consequence: later explanations, measurements, datasets, methods, or decisions.
Field/time-qualified citations measure some uptake and attention; record follow-up windows and missed forms of use (Bornmann and Daniel 2008; Waltman 2016; Petersen et al. 2025).
Keep predicted impact dated and separate from realized impact; an overlooked gain can still be an advance (Wang et al. 2017).



Uptake

Uptake is impact counted on the unit of novelty: the later reuse of one specific new element. Hofstra counts, for each new concept link a thesis introduced, how many later theses use that link (Hofstra et al. 2020). Citations per paper, Uzzi’s outcome, count attention to the whole paper, not reuse of its new part (Uzzi et al. 2013).
Impactful novelty is novelty that is taken up. Hofstra models uptake only where novelty is greater than zero, so “not adopted” is not confused with “nothing to adopt” (Hofstra et al. 2020).
Innovation = novelty × uptake, kept as two variables. The split lets two separate questions be asked: who creates new links, and whose links spread. In Hofstra’s data they have opposite answers. Scholars with fewer demographically similar peers introduce more new links, and their links are reused less (Hofstra et al. 2020).
Before- and after-the-fact estimates of uptake are different quantities. Si’s “excitement” rating is a reviewer’s estimate before the work is done of “potential impact and influence if developed fully” (Si et al. 2025). Hofstra’s uptake is observed afterwards. The advance profile keeps the two in separate fields.



Breadth, interdisciplinarity, and depth

Breadth is a candidate contributor to advance: test when integrating another field’s concepts, methods, or observations helps (Wagner et al. 2011; Shi and Evans 2023).
Distinguish project integration, competent individual/team reach, and diversity across a portfolio. Reference diversity alone demonstrates none of these.
Depth means demonstrated competence and understanding. Reference concentration and topic specialization are proxies for concentration, not its definition (Teodoridis et al. 2019; Rassenfosse et al. 2022).
Empirical studies differ in populations and outcomes: citation combinations (Uzzi et al. 2013), career costs/uptake (Leahey et al. 2017), and scientific AI/topic coverage (Hao et al. 2026). A writing experiment (Doshi and Hauser 2024) is a different setting. No combined universal breadth recipe follows.
Breadth of inputs and distance of a link are measured differently. Reference diversity measures what was read, over the whole reference list (Stirling 2007; Wagner et al. 2011). Distal novelty measures how far apart two joined concepts are, one link at a time (Hofstra et al. 2020). A paper can read broadly and join nothing distant.



Field-shaping

Retrospective change in a field’s questions, capabilities, practices, or explanatory resources.
Citation disruption, canonical status, and delayed recognition observe different aspects (Wu et al. 2019; Petersen et al. 2025; Chu and Evans 2021; Ke et al. 2015).
Enabling is a contribution role, not a middle rank between incremental and field-shaping.
Field-shaping differs from uptake in what is counted. Uptake counts reuse of a new element. Field-shaping asks whether the later literature reorganized around the work: whether its citers stop citing what it built on (Funk and Owen-Smith 2017; Wu et al. 2019), whether the field’s canon turns over (Chu and Evans 2021), or whether recognition arrives late and from another field (Ke et al. 2015). A widely reused link can leave a field’s structure unchanged; a paper cited little for a decade can reshape one.
Uzzi’s high-impact profile, a conventional base with an intrusion of atypical combinations (Uzzi et al. 2013), is a claim about citation impact, not about field-shaping. Meeting 10 recorded it as “a strong base and a niche where you add the novelty.”

title: Scientific advance and modes of inquiry
text:
Action, commitment, and claim status







Distinction
Record and evaluate




Action restriction
Does a rule require a hypothesis before every next action? Treat this as a policy to test, not a premise.


Prospective commitment
What was fixed, when, before access to which evaluation evidence? Record amendments, blinding, unknown, and not applicable (Nosek et al. 2018).


Claim warrant
Does the asserted scope/status match the evidence supplied for this kind of claim? Allow conjectures and provisional findings.




A frozen forecast, blinded test, and registered analysis plan are related but distinct. Data can already exist before a legitimate prospective commitment about access or analysis.
Ioannidis models false-positive risks under assumptions; it does not prescribe a universal hypothesis-before-action rule (Ioannidis 2005).
A turning point may be identifiable, but published narrative is not complete chronology. Separate raw artifacts, contemporaneous statements, and retrospective interpretations (Holmes 1987).
Revise a definition by recording the case it fails on and the changed version. An agent can suggest revisions; it cannot silently redefine its evaluation criteria.

title: Modes of inquiry: definitions, evidence, and the graph
text:
Central question
Which kinds of scientific work does an agent family need, where was each defined, and has any been shown to raise novelty, breadth, or advance?


Anchor
Elliott et al. (2016), full text, open access. Read “A richer account of scientific practice” and their Figure 3.


Companion
Betts et al. (2021), open access. The rotating reader presents the coding scheme and Figure 4.


Geoscience pair, optional
Pfister and Kirchner (2017) and Baker (2017), the Water Resources Research debate on hypothesis testing in hydrology.


Bring
One paper of your own, with its modes named in order from the table in section 2.


Output
A decision on the mode list (keep, split, merge, add), each with the source that forces it; graph v0.4 adopted, amended, or rejected; one ledger row.




Why these two: Elliott and colleagues name plural modes and judge research by “the alignment between the nature of the knowledge gap or challenge addressed and the combination of approaches or methods used” (Elliott et al. 2016). Betts and colleagues coded 268 ecology and evolution papers, found multiple alternative hypotheses in 6.7% and no citation or grant advantage for any hypothesis use, and still argue for more of it (Betts et al. 2021).
One conceptual, one empirical, and they disagree: Elliott judges by fit to the knowledge gap, Betts by the clarity that rival hypotheses bring. Neither is geoscience; the optional pair is.

title: Modes of inquiry: definitions, evidence, and the graph
text:
1. What a mode is

Working definition. A mode of inquiry is a kind of epistemic work, named by the gain it aims at and the evidence its claims owe. It describes an episode or an action, not a whole paper.
Precedent for the word. O’Malley, Elliott, and Burian name four modes of research practice: hypothesis-driven, exploratory, question-driven, and technology-oriented Elliott (2012). Moving back and forth between them is “methodological iteration” (Elliott 2012).
Not the same as:




Term
Unit
Source
Relation to our modes




Style of reasoning
A long-lived tradition: six in Crombie, plus a laboratory and an “algorismic” style in Hacking
Crombie (1988); Hacking (2002)
Coarser; one style holds several modes


Epistemic culture
A field’s machinery for making knowledge
Knorr Cetina (1999)
Orthogonal; a culture uses many modes


Paradigm, in Gray’s sense
An era: empirical, theoretical, computational, data-intensive
Hey et al. (2009)
A period label; the fourth spans three of our modes


Mode 1 / Mode 2
How knowledge production is organized
glossary
Term collision only


Method, in this book
A composition of units on the graph
unit, section 6
How a mode runs the graph


Contribution type
What a paper delivers: data, estimate, method, concept
glossary
The output, not the work




How modes relate, four claims in the literature:

Historical sequence, cumulative: Crombie’s order of emergence; Gray’s four paradigms (Crombie 1988; Hey et al. 2009).
Coexistence with unequal stability: “The taxonomic and the historic-genetic styles have produced nothing like the stability of the laboratory or the mathematical style” (Hacking 2002).
Iteration: data- and technology-driven programmes are “complementary and iterative partners” of hypothesis-led work (Kell and Oliver 2004, 99; Elliott 2012; Elliott et al. 2016).
Institutional hierarchy: some funders privilege hypothesis testing (O’Malley et al. 2009, 612–13; Haufe 2013), as do US courts judging scientific testimony (Haufe 2013, 364); school science teaches the single-variable experiment (Manduca and Kastens 2012, 2). Haufe’s reason: hypothesis testing is the easiest to appraise, not the best (p. 366).

The book adopts iteration. The hierarchy is a claim about practice, and section 5 tests it.

title: Modes of inquiry: definitions, evidence, and the graph
section: 2. Thirteen definitions and where they come from
text:
2. Thirteen definitions and where they come from









Mode
Gain it aims at
Defined as distinct work by
Contested boundary




Question-driven inquiry
A question framed so that some result would answer it, and reframed when a pass ends without a conclusion
Named only by O’Malley et al. (2009) and O’Malley et al. (2010), with Elliott (2012); parts of a question from Fraassen (1980) and Nickles (1981)
No evidence standard in the mode literature; the seminar assembles one


Observation and description
A credible record of a phenomenon, its variability, and what is unobserved
Data versus phenomena (Bogen and Woodward 1988); “‘Descriptive’ in science is a pejorative, almost always preceded by ‘merely’” (Grimaldi and Engel 2007)
No peer-reviewed account gives description its own success criteria


Exploratory inquiry
Phenomena, questions, and representations
Experimentation “not … driven by specific theories” (Steinle 1997, S65); “mapping activities” (Franklin 2005, 893); extended to observational data (Pietsch 2015, 914)
Steinle’s exploration aims at regularities, so it overlaps the last row


Hypothesis assessment
Discrimination among rivals
“He invents hypotheses and he invents tests for them” (Gilbert 1896, 2); the smoking gun (Cleland 2002, 480)
Generation and test are separate actions, already in Gilbert


Theory and mechanistic modeling
Concepts, explanations, valid derivations
Models as mediating instruments (Morrison and Morgan 1999); modeling is “indirect representation and analysis” (Weisberg 2007, 207)
Weisberg separates modeling from other theorizing; our row joins them


Simulation and prediction
Computed consequences; assessed forecasts
“A new kind of scientific method” (Humphreys 2004); Winsberg (2010); prediction as a goal (Shmueli 2010)
Computer simulation studies are “material experiments in a straightforward sense,” though simulations as such are not (Parker 2009, 483, 495); the row joins a method with a goal


Instruments and observing systems
A reliable new measurement capability
Experimentation “has a life of its own” (Hacking 1983, 150); instruments “express knowledge” (Baird 2004); Rheinberger (2011)
Merged with methods as “technology-oriented” (O’Malley et al. 2009, 612; 2010)


Methods and computation
A new inference or computational capability
No source defines it as a mode. Nearest: the algorismic style “dedicated to finding algorithms” (Hacking 2002); tools that become theories (Gigerenzer 1991)
Gap


Cross-study synthesis
A pooled estimate or a connection across studies that no single study supports
Meta-analysis (Gurevitch et al. 2018); synthesis centres (Carpenter et al. 2009)
Where pooling ends and a new estimate begins


Reconstruction from traces
A constrained history of a past event, retained against stated rival histories
Historical science (Cleland 2002); prehistory from traces (Turner 2007)
Whether convergent traces confirm or only explain


Replication and robustness
What survives repetition, perturbation, transfer
Replication: Schmidt (2009); Machery (2020). Robustness: Wimsatt (2012); Parker (2011)
Defined for experiments and model ensembles. Nearest for a one-off natural event: conceptual replication, a test of the hypothesis “with different methods” (Schmidt 2009, 91)


Inferential estimation
A latent quantity with uncertainty and resolution
Backus and Gilbert (1968) (resolution); Tarantola (2005) (uncertainty); inversion in philosophy: Bokulich and Oreskes (2017)
Absent from every general taxonomy


Statistical modeling and empirical regularities
A relation or distribution with a warranted range
Crombie’s style (e) (Hacking 2002); two cultures (Breiman 2001); descriptive versus explanatory models (Shmueli 2010)
Overlaps exploration




Three modes have no source that defines them as a distinct mode: methods and computation, inferential estimation, and replication for non-repeatable natural events, where conceptual replication is the nearest (Schmidt 2009, 91). Estimation is where geophysics wrote its own founding texts (Backus and Gilbert 1968; Tarantola 2005); its only philosophical treatment is Bokulich and Oreskes (2017).
Missing relative to the precedents: question-driven inquiry (O’Malley et al. 2010) and systematic invention, or engineering design (Pickstone 2007). The book keeps question origin as a ledger attribute (decided September 10, 2026). O’Malley and colleagues are the case against that decision.
Proposed for the room: split synthesis. Research synthesis across studies and reconstruction from traces owe different evidence (study selection versus common-cause inference), and no precedent joins them. One agent system was 85.5% accurate on its data-analysis statements and 57.9% on its synthesis statements (Mitchener et al. 2025, preprint).
Geoscience accounts agree on three points: explanatory pluralism, narrative with causal explanation (Kleinhans et al. 2005); several rivals at once (Gilbert 1896; Cleland 2002); model-laden data (Bokulich and Oreskes 2017; Bokulich 2020). They differ on how far laboratory accounts fit: geoscience tests hypotheses, but against observations and through “multiple converging lines of evidence” rather than single-variable experiments (Manduca and Kastens 2012, 1–2), or field work does not fit a philosophy built on the laboratory (Raab and Frodeman 2002; Baker 2017).

Read from abstracts only: Leahey et al. (2023), Wren (2016). Miranda and Garcia-Carpintero (2018), Patsopoulos et al. (2005), Fawcett and Higginson (2012), and Bartneck and Rauterberg (2008) were checked against the full text on October 20, 2026. The rest were read in full or in an open preprint; the private analysis lists the basis per source.
Correctness and citation pull apart. Citations do not reflect soundness or originality (Aksnes et al. 2019); the replication rows show it directly.
Breadth is measured in topics and references, not modes. A pivot away from one’s own past references cuts the top-5% hit rate from 7.4% to 2.2% (Hill et al. 2025); publishing into a distant audience makes a hit 3.5 times as likely (Shi and Evans 2023); generalists or specialists win depending on the field’s pace (Teodoridis et al. 2019). A hypothesis neither paper tests: carrying a home method to a distant audience is an expedition, not a pivot.
What travels and what stays. Methods, instruments, and model templates cross fields; validation standards and task routines stay behind (MacLeod 2018).
One person, two modes. Bimodal modeler-experimenters reported losing time switching, and their field doubted it could become the norm (MacLeod and Nersessian 2016, 409).
Teams of different approaches. Diversity helps on rugged problems and costs speed; on smooth problems the best performers win (Hong and Page 2004; Grim et al. 2019, 108; Thoma 2015; Wu and O’Connor 2023). The gain in Weisberg and Muldoon’s model is the mavericks’ own work (Weisberg and Muldoon 2009; Alexander et al. 2015, 440).

Claims this evidence does not support.

That hypothesis-driven papers have more impact (Betts et al. 2021).
That most breakthroughs follow hypothesis testing: 81% of 761 major discoveries used it, with no comparison set (Krauss 2024).
That science is driven more by tools than ideas: the counts flip with the coding (Greenwald 2012; Bartneck and Rauterberg 2008).
That being cited means being correct (Serra-Garcia and Gneezy 2021; Aksnes et al. 2019).
That breadth in modes raises impact: no study measures it.
That any of this holds in the Earth sciences: no impact study above uses an Earth-science corpus.

title: Modes of inquiry: definitions, evidence, and the graph
text:
6. From modes to agents

No taxonomy of AI in science is organized by mode. Surveys sort by workflow stage, autonomy, or mechanism (Zheng et al. 2025; Reddy and Shojaee 2025); one sorts by kind of understanding (Krenn et al. 2022). The nearest to a mode list is the five geoscience problem classes of Karpatne et al. (2019).
Coverage. Coded by this search over 19 published systems and benchmarks: the core loop runs methods in 7, hypothesis generation and ranking in 6, regularities in 4, literature synthesis in 4, and simulation, instruments, or replication in none. All 19 start from a supplied goal; none starts from an anomaly or reconstructs an event from physical traces.
Roles. One multi-agent system splits agents by epistemic function: generation, reflection, ranking, evolution (Gottweis et al. 2026). Others split by disciplinary persona, career rank, or tool (Swanson et al. 2025; Su et al. 2025; Schmidgall et al. 2025; Ghareeb et al. 2026).
Drift. AI-augmented papers concentrate where data are abundant, topics shrink by 4.63%, and follow-on engagement falls by 22%; the authors read it as a move from questions of origin to operational ones, which they did not measure by mode (Hao et al. 2026). Against it, LLM adopters cite 11.9% more books (Kusumegi et al. 2025).









Design hypothesis
Evidence for
What would refute it




Specialize agents by the evidence a mode owes, not by persona or by Peirce’s labels
Search access for the reflection agent cut implausible hypotheses (Gottweis et al. 2026); agents split by abduction, deduction, and induction were tested only on logic puzzles (Abdaljalil et al. 2025)
A generalist with the same tools and budget runs as many mode-specific checks as the specialists


Each mode agent has an evaluator the generating model does not control
Automated reviewers scored 6.1 of 10 against 3.8 from humans (Schmidgall et al. 2025); the A-Lab scored itself (Leeman et al. 2024)
Self-scores track blinded expert scores


Synthesis is its own agent, scored apart from the analyses it draws on
57.9% against 85.5% accuracy (Mitchener et al. 2025)
Synthesis accuracy equals analysis accuracy once scored separately


A system without a mode budget drifts to data-rich modes
Hao et al. (2026); the coverage counts above
Logged mode shares in the group’s runs match the ledger without a budget


A method carried to a new field must carry that field’s validation standard
MacLeod (2018); the Ising model lost its renormalization-group warrant moving from physics to socio-economics (Knuuttila and Loettgers 2016)
Transferred methods pass the destination’s checks without being given them


Specialists built on one base model are not a diverse team
Diversity’s advantage depends on solvers that differ (Hong and Page 2004; Grim et al. 2019)
Same-model specialists generate as many distinct rivals as specialists on different models


The exploration agent enters from an anomaly
None of the 19 systems does; Kosmos “can sometimes veer in unexpected trajectories” (Mitchener et al. 2025, 19)
An agent given a goal finds the anomalies an anomaly-entry agent finds




The polymath hypothesis, restated for agents. A human’s cost of holding two modes is training and switching time (MacLeod and Nersessian 2016); an agent’s switching cost is near zero. That is where a generalist could beat people. Test: one generalist agent against a team of three mode specialists on a task that needs simulation and observation, scored by a blinded specialist in each mode, recording whether each mode’s own checks ran.

7. For the room

Decided by the convenor (October 21, 2026): synthesis split, question-driven inquiry added. For the room: does any other mode need splitting?
Is methods and computation a mode or a contribution type? Hacking gives it a style; no one gives it its own warrant.
Graph v0.4: do E, N, and I place your own paper better than v0.3 did?
Which outcome should a mode agent be scored on, by whom, and against what baseline?


Exercise. Code your paper by mode, draw it as a path on the decision tree, and mark the node where its decisive move happened. Then do the same for one row of the episode table and compare.
Record. Sign the notes; one ledger row; the decision on the list and on graph v0.4, with the source behind each change.

That any mode causes novelty, breadth, or advance.

title: Question-driven inquiry
text:
Epistemic purpose
Drafted human-editable specification · v0.1.0 · added on October 21, 2026 by convenor decision · no agent-performance claim

title: Question-driven inquiry
text: Pose, sharpen, or reframe a research question, and pursue it through partial answers that change the aim, rather than testing a hypothesis already stated. The product is a better-posed question: what it presupposes, which alternatives count as answers, the constraints an answer must meet, and the partial answers that justified each change.

title: Question-driven inquiry
text:
When this mode helps

At the start, when a project has a topic or a programmatic question (“What is an earthquake?” (National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine 2020, 19)) but no question a result could answer.
In the decision tree, at question 8, when a pass ends without a conclusion: the question is reframed and the project re-enters the tree at the start.
Not this mode: generating rival answers to a question already posed, which is hypothesis assessment or theory.

title: Question-driven inquiry
text:
Agent actions and representations

Write the question with its parts: the presupposition (what must be true for the question to have an answer), the contrast class (the alternatives an answer chooses among), the relevance relation, and the constraints on an acceptable answer (Fraassen 1980; Nickles 1981; Hintikka 1981).
Translate it into slots that can be checked, after the clinical PICO form (Richardson et al. 1995): object, contrast, observable, window.
When reframing after no conclusion, diagnose first: insufficient power, a measurement problem, the wrong representation, the wrong rivals, or a false presupposition. Then choose a move: change the representation or search space (Klahr and Simon 1999); widen or narrow the answer space (Elliott 2012); challenge an assumption of the literature (Alvesson and Sandberg 2011; Sandberg and Alvesson 2011).
Inputs: the record (the schema terms), the failed pass and its diagnosis, the budget.
Outputs: the question before and after, the diagnosis, the move used, and a claim record when the reframing itself is a claim (for example, that a presupposition is false).

title: Question-driven inquiry
text:
Evidence and claim scope

A question is good when one can say, before the work, which outcomes would answer it, a contradiction included (Glass 2010). It is narrower than a problem agenda (Love 2008) and wider than a hypothesis, which is one candidate answer put up for test.
A reframing owes: both questions written in full; the diagnosis of why the pass did not conclude; which assumption or constraint changed; a search showing the new question has not already been answered, run against the question and not only a method; and a flag when the same data will answer the new question, because that pass is then exploratory, not confirmatory.
A false presupposition shown false is a conclusion, and so a success, not a failure.

title: Question-driven inquiry
text:
Transitions and stopping

Hands the reframed question to the start of the tree: exploration when the phenomenon itself is in doubt, hypothesis assessment when rivals can now be named.
Proposed stopping rule (open for the room). One reframing per pass. A second only if the first produced a partial answer and changed the contrast class or a constraint so that the question now predicts an observation the old one did not; this is Lakatos’s progressive problemshift applied to questions (Lakatos 1970). Stop as a success when a pass concludes or a presupposition is shown false. Stop as a failure, recorded with both questions and the diagnosis, when a reframing changes only the wording, or after two reframings without a conclusion. No source sets the number two.

title: Question-driven inquiry
text:
Characteristic failure

Reword the question without changing what would answer it; frame a broad inquiry after the fact as a narrow hypothesis test (O’Malley et al. 2009, 611); spot a gap without asking whether the assumption behind it holds (Sandberg and Alvesson 2011); check a new question’s novelty against methods only.

title: Question-driven inquiry
text:
Human evidence and borrowing

Named as a mode only by O’Malley and colleagues: “open-ended and nonlinear approaches” whose inquiries “ramify as successive investigations produce partial answers that modify the original aim” (O’Malley et al. 2009, 612); and in their four modes of research practice (O’Malley et al. 2010), from which Elliott defines methodological iteration as moving “back and forth between different modes” (Elliott 2012). None of the three gives the mode an evidence standard; the criteria above are the seminar’s synthesis.
What a research question is. Philosophy treats the problem (a question with constraints and a demand for a solution: Nickles (1981); Klahr and Simon (1999)) and the question itself (presupposition, contrast class, admissible answers: Fraassen (1980); Hintikka (1981)). Clinical research makes evaluation usable: PICO (Richardson et al. 1995). Organization studies show that most published questions fill gaps rather than challenge assumptions (Sandberg and Alvesson 2011). For Earth science, the national surveys pose programmatic questions (National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine 2020), from which project questions have to be derived.
What a research idea is. In the AI ideation literature an idea is a proposal that already holds a candidate answer and a test: problem, method, and experiment plan (Si et al. 2025; Baek et al. 2025; Wang et al. 2024), or a goal turned into hypotheses (Gottweis et al. 2026; Lu et al. 2026). An idea therefore comes after a question; its novelty is checked against methods, never against whether the question was already answered.
Why funders prefer hypotheses: hypothesis testing “is relatively easy to appraise” (Haufe 2013, 363); Glass (2010) defends the question as the frame for an experiment.
Failure as no conclusion. Most measures count null results, which are conclusions when powered. 37.3% of results presented in biomedical abstracts reach full publication (Scherer et al. 2018); null findings are mostly not written up (Franco et al. 2014); registered reports report 60% null hypotheses (Chambers and Tzavella 2022). In geophysics, 69 of 217 NSF awards from 2015 in the Geophysics program list no publication, an upper bound on non-publication, not a failure rate (NSF award API, queried October 21, 2026).
The actions above are design hypotheses derived from these sources, not established optimal policies.

title: Question-driven inquiry
text:
Evaluation against past work

Given a project’s original proposal and its outcome report, an agent states the question in full, diagnoses why it did or did not conclude, and proposes a reframing; assessors judge whether the reframing changes what would answer the question. Candidate corpus: NSF Earth-science awards with a Project Outcomes Report but no publication.

title: Observation and description
text:
Epistemic purpose
Drafted human-editable specification · v0.4.3 · no agent-performance claim

title: Observation and description
text: Establish a credible record of a phenomenon, its variability, and what remains unobserved.

title: Observation and description
text:
When this mode helps

A survey, catalog, map, or time series addresses a scientific uncertainty. Record detection, coverage, and missingness; do not treat a processing output as a direct observation of every inferred quantity.

title: Observation and description
text:
Agent actions and representations

Inspect metadata; map coverage; characterize distributions; compare recording conditions; identify gaps; choose the next observation under a resource budget.
Inputs: the question, available evidence and provenance, constraints, prior claims, and remaining budget.
Outputs: inspectable artifacts, updated question/evidence state, and a claim record when a substantive claim is made.

title: Observation and description
text:
Evidence and claim scope

Coverage, completeness, measurement response, and traceable processing must support the descriptive scope. A unique event can be documented even when the event cannot recur.
Distinguish a warranted decision at the time from a claim’s later assessed adequacy; append follow-up without rewriting the original record.

title: Observation and description
text:
Transitions and stopping

If a pattern needs characterization, enter exploration; if the target is latent, enter estimation; if the observation chain is suspect, enter instrumentation or robustness.
Neighbouring profiles: exploration, estimation, instruments, robustness.

title: Observation and description
text:
Characteristic failure

Coverage or detection thresholds masquerade as physical patterns; an exhaustive catalog produces no gain relevant to the question.

title: Observation and description
text:
Human evidence and borrowing

Primary cases: coastal traces in Atwater (1987) and observing programs in Becker et al. (2019). Bogen and Woodward (1988) offers the philosophical distinction between data and phenomena. These sources motivate the profile; they do not validate an agent policy.
Cross-field comparison: Compare catalog practices with exploratory high-energy physics in Karaca (2013a) and its correction Karaca (2013b); transfer attention to observation conditions, not the physics.
Science of process/impact: Fortunato et al. (2018) supplies broad metascience context. Mode prevalence and gains from this procedure in geoscience have not been estimated here.
Definition and evidence (modes meeting, drafted October 2026): Defined as distinct work by the data/phenomena distinction (Bogen and Woodward 1988) and a defence of description against “merely” (Grimaldi and Engel 2007); no peer-reviewed source gives description its own success criteria. Curated ocean data sets out-cite 99% of oceanography articles (Belter 2014). On graph v0.4: O (observe) and E (explore: establish the phenomenon), often after N (new capability).
The actions and transitions above are design hypotheses derived from these sources, not established optimal policies. Missing process chronology remains unknown.

title: Observation and description
text:
Evaluation against past work

A case gains an adequately characterized feature or resolves a consequential coverage limitation. Test a catalog with changed detection sensitivity; require a justified next observation, not a fictitious new phenomenon.
Use the historical evaluation to choose a source record, preserve evidence boundaries, and assess a meaningful gain. A synthetic control tests a constructed case, not a historical discovery.

title: Exploratory inquiry
text:
Epistemic purpose
Drafted human-editable specification · v0.4.3 · no agent-performance claim

title: Exploratory inquiry
text: Develop phenomena, questions, candidate relationships, and useful representations.

title: Exploratory inquiry
text:
When this mode helps

The question, target phenomenon, or representation is still developing. Background theory and provisional hypotheses may be present; absence of a hypothesis is not the recognition rule.

title: Exploratory inquiry
text:
Agent actions and representations

Inspect and visualize; vary conditions; compare representations; follow anomalies; generate candidates; frame or reframe questions; preserve abandoned branches and search history.
Inputs: the question, available evidence and provenance, constraints, prior claims, and remaining budget.
Outputs: inspectable artifacts, updated question/evidence state, and a claim record when a substantive claim is made.

title: Exploratory inquiry
text:
Evidence and claim scope

A provisional pattern needs credible provenance and an appropriate initial reliability check. Stronger generalization needs further evidence. Record which data suggested the pattern; do not present that inspection as a prospective test.
Distinguish a warranted decision at the time from a claim’s later assessed adequacy; append follow-up without rewriting the original record.

title: Exploratory inquiry
text:
Transitions and stopping

Investigate possible artifacts through instruments or robustness; estimate a developed observable; assess rival explanations when they make distinguishable predictions. Stop or reframe when follow-up has low scientific value under the budget.
Neighbouring profiles: observation, estimation, hypothesis, instruments, robustness.

title: Exploratory inquiry
text:
Characteristic failure

Reject a unique event before investigating it; mistake a selection artifact for a finding; retrofit an exploratory outcome as a prediction.

title: Exploratory inquiry
text:
Human evidence and borrowing

Steinle (1997) and Karaca (2013a) are historical/philosophical analyses of exploratory practice; consult Karaca (2013b). Rouet-Leduc et al. (2017) is a geoscience case for distinguishing discovery from subsequent assessment.
Cross-field comparison: The high-energy physics case informs variation and representation change. The transferable procedure is an explicit question, not a claim that all exploration is theory-free.
Science of process/impact: Yaqub (2018) organizes serendipity; Foster et al. (2015) measures research strategies in biomedicine. Neither establishes the gain from this specific geoscience agent policy.
Definition and evidence (modes meeting, drafted October 2026): Defined as experimentation “not … driven by specific theories” (Steinle 1997, S65), as mapping (Franklin 2005, 893), and for observational data (Pietsch 2015). Exploration-tolerant funding raised both hits and flops (Azoulay et al. 2011). None of 19 published agent systems coded for the modes meeting enters from an anomaly. On graph v0.4: E (explore: establish the phenomenon), looping with O (observe).
The actions and transitions above are design hypotheses derived from these sources, not established optimal policies. Missing process chronology remains unknown.

title: Exploratory inquiry
text:
Evaluation against past work

Produce a credible candidate and a discriminating follow-up that could advance the question. Compare a real-looking artifact with an unusual valid observation; report candidate quality and follow-up usefulness separately from confirmed advance.
Use the historical evaluation to choose a source record, preserve evidence boundaries, and assess a meaningful gain. A synthetic control tests a constructed case, not a historical discovery.

title: Hypothesis assessment
text:
Epistemic purpose
Drafted human-editable specification · v0.4.4 · no agent-performance claim

title: Hypothesis assessment
text: Discriminate among explanations or stated expectations using informative evidence.

title: Hypothesis assessment
text:
When this mode helps

The scientific question concerns alternatives that can have different evidential consequences. Rival generation and discrimination are separate actions.

title: Hypothesis assessment
text:
Agent actions and representations

Generate substantive rivals; identify auxiliary assumptions; derive differing predictions; choose a discriminating observation; compare results; revise the rival set when needed.
Inputs: the question, available evidence and provenance, constraints, prior claims, and remaining budget.
Outputs: inspectable artifacts, updated question/evidence state, and a claim record when a substantive claim is made.

title: Hypothesis assessment
text:
Evidence and claim scope

State what each outcome supports and what remains unresolved. Evidence need not exclude every imaginable rival to support a bounded claim; shared assumptions and untested alternatives limit its strength.
Distinguish a warranted decision at the time from a claim’s later assessed adequacy; append follow-up without rewriting the original record.

title: Hypothesis assessment
text:
Transitions and stopping

Reframe or return to exploration when all rivals accommodate the available evidence; acquire a new observable; use estimation to quantify the predicted contrast.
Neighbouring profiles: exploration, theory, estimation, simulation, synthesis.

title: Hypothesis assessment
text:
Characteristic failure

Verbal variants masquerade as rivals; all alternatives pass the proposed test; an auxiliary assumption absorbs every failure; a causal claim outruns an association.
The absorbing auxiliary is the Duhem problem (Duhem 1954; Quine 1951): a failed prediction refutes the conjunction of hypothesis, auxiliaries, and conditions, and logic does not say which to drop. This mode runs the whole loop of the unit graph; record at node X which conjunct was revised and why.

title: Hypothesis assessment
text:
Human evidence and borrowing

Platt (1964) offers a methodological argument; Cleland (2001) and Cleland (2002) distinguish historical and experimental reasoning. Sykes (1967) is the primary tectonic test case, not a controlled evaluation of agents.
Cross-field comparison: King et al. (2009) illustrates executable hypothesis testing in yeast with assay constraints; borrowing requires identifying which geoscience observations can play the comparable discriminating role.
Science of process/impact: Si et al. (2025) distinguishes idea ratings from executed research outcomes in NLP. Its results motivate testing rival quality through consequences rather than fluent phrasing.
Definition and evidence (modes meeting, drafted October 2026): Defined by Gilbert: the investigator “invents hypotheses and he invents tests for them” (Gilbert 1896, 2). Hypothesis use carried no citation or grant advantage in 268 ecology and evolution papers (Betts et al. 2021); 21 of 100 ecology papers tested more than one hypothesis (Betini et al. 2017). In 18 coded geoscience advances it did decisive work in 7, usually late (modes meeting). On graph v0.4: H (generate hypotheses), S, D (design the test), C (compare), X (exclude), P (protect), R (refine): the whole hypothesis pass.
The actions and transitions above are design hypotheses derived from these sources, not established optimal policies. Missing process chronology remains unknown.

title: Hypothesis assessment
text:
Evaluation against past work

Resolve a scientifically important contrast or demonstrate why current evidence cannot. Include distinguishable rivals, equifinal rivals, and a missing-data case; score gain and unsupported exclusions.
Use the historical evaluation to choose a source record, preserve evidence boundaries, and assess a meaningful gain. A synthetic control tests a constructed case, not a historical discovery.
Assessment definitions · Agent implementation

title: Theory and mechanistic modeling
text:
Epistemic purpose
Drafted human-editable specification · v0.4.4 · no agent-performance claim

title: Theory and mechanistic modeling
text: Create concepts, explanations, and derivations that make new relationships understandable or testable.

title: Theory and mechanistic modeling
text:
When this mode helps

A concept, mechanism, or formal representation changes what can be explained or derived. Observation may precede or motivate theory.

title: Theory and mechanistic modeling
text:
Agent actions and representations

Construct representations; propose mechanisms; derive consequences; inspect limiting cases and dimensions; compare explanatory scope; identify measurements that distinguish applications.
Inputs: the question, available evidence and provenance, constraints, prior claims, and remaining budget.
Outputs: inspectable artifacts, updated question/evidence state, and a claim record when a substantive claim is made.

title: Theory and mechanistic modeling
text:
Evidence and claim scope

Assess mathematical validity under explicit assumptions separately from empirical adequacy. A sound derivation does not require an observation to have already occurred; its application to a system requires additional evidence.
Distinguish a warranted decision at the time from a claim’s later assessed adequacy; append follow-up without rewriting the original record.

title: Theory and mechanistic modeling
text:
Transitions and stopping

Use simulation when consequences need computation; enter hypothesis assessment when mechanisms have distinct observable consequences; revise representation after incompatibility.
Neighbouring profiles: exploration, simulation, hypothesis, synthesis.

title: Theory and mechanistic modeling
text:
Characteristic failure

Treat internal consistency as empirical truth; demand prospective prediction as the only route to theory; equate an elegant narrative with a derived consequence.

title: Theory and mechanistic modeling
text:
Human evidence and borrowing

Wilson (1965) and Vine and Matthews (1963) are conceptual/physical cases; Dellsén (2016) and Bird (2007) supply contrasting accounts of scientific progress. The profile is a proposed operational interpretation.
Cross-field comparison: Nersessian (2022) supplies a bioengineering comparison for building and adapting representations; record what assumptions survive the change of domain.
Science of process/impact: Fortunato et al. (2018) reviews metascience at broader scales. No measured geoscience benefit of this theory procedure is claimed.
Definition and evidence (modes meeting, drafted October 2026): Defined through models as mediating instruments (Morrison and Morgan 1999) and modeling as “indirect representation and analysis” (Weisberg 2007, 207); Weisberg separates what this profile joins. Model templates cross fields; within physics the renormalization group carries their warrant, across disciplines it may not (Knuuttila and Loettgers 2016, 377, 380; 2023). Weisberg files Darwin’s atoll theory as theorizing without models (p. 227). New theories are less disruptive than new methods (Leahey et al. (2023), abstract). On graph v0.4: H (generate hypotheses) and S (derive or simulate).
The actions and transitions above are design hypotheses derived from these sources, not established optimal policies. Missing process chronology remains unknown.

title: Theory and mechanistic modeling
text:
Evaluation against past work

Demonstrate a valid new consequence, explanatory connection, or capability relative to the task. Include a derivation with a hidden inconsistent assumption and a valid idealization with a limited empirical scope.
Use the historical evaluation to choose a source record, preserve evidence boundaries, and assess a meaningful gain. A synthetic control tests a constructed case, not a historical discovery.
Assessment definitions · Agent implementation

title: Simulation and prediction
text:
Epistemic purpose
Drafted human-editable specification · v0.4.4 · no agent-performance claim

title: Simulation and prediction
text: Compute model consequences, investigate scenarios, or make assessed forecasts.

title: Simulation and prediction
text:
When this mode helps

Separate scenario exploration from a predictive claim. Inferring a latent parameter belongs to estimation even when a forward simulator is used.

title: Simulation and prediction
text:
Agent actions and representations

Specify governing assumptions and boundary conditions; check numerics; run sensitivity or scenario analysis; produce forecasts and uncertainty; freeze predictions before evaluation evidence is accessed.
Inputs: the question, available evidence and provenance, constraints, prior claims, and remaining budget.
Outputs: inspectable artifacts, updated question/evidence state, and a claim record when a substantive claim is made.

title: Simulation and prediction
text:
Evidence and claim scope

Numerical verification, purpose, and uncertainty support computational claims. Predictive skill requires a suitable baseline and independent assessment; scenario calculations do not become forecasts merely by producing numbers.
Distinguish a warranted decision at the time from a claim’s later assessed adequacy; append follow-up without rewriting the original record.

title: Simulation and prediction
text:
Transitions and stopping

Enter estimation for unknown parameters, hypothesis assessment for competing models, or robustness when performance depends on conditions; revise model purpose if evidence cannot support the intended claim.
Neighbouring profiles: estimation, hypothesis, robustness, theory.

title: Simulation and prediction
text:
Characteristic failure

Treat fit as truth, simulation as a physical experiment, or agreement among related models as independent evidence.

title: Simulation and prediction
text:
Human evidence and borrowing

Oreskes et al. (1994) distinguishes partial confirmation from complete verification/validation of natural-system models; Beven and Freer (2001) treats equifinality; Schorlemmer et al. (2018) describes earthquake-forecast evaluation.
Cross-field comparison: Shmueli (2010) distinguishes explanatory and predictive objectives across statistical applications. Borrow the distinction while retaining domain-specific physical checks.
Science of process/impact: No corpus result is available for this profile. Forecast scores quantify particular predictive gains and do not measure every kind of advance.
Definition and evidence (modes meeting, drafted October 2026): Defined as a new kind of method (Humphreys 2004; Winsberg 2010); computer simulation studies, though not simulations as such, as material experiments (Parker 2009, 483, 495). Unmeasured as a contribution type in the science of science, and the core loop of none of 19 published agent systems coded for the modes meeting. The forecast-verification composition is from Charney et al. (1950). On graph v0.4: S (derive or simulate), and C (compare) in the forecast-verification composition.
The actions and transitions above are design hypotheses derived from these sources, not established optimal policies. Missing process chronology remains unknown.

title: Simulation and prediction
text:
Evaluation against past work

Compare forecasts with a stated baseline on held-out observations; retain scenario usefulness as a separate assessment. Test a model with good fitting error and poor transfer.
Use the historical evaluation to choose a source record, preserve evidence boundaries, and assess a meaningful gain. A synthetic control tests a constructed case, not a historical discovery.
Assessment definitions · Agent implementation

title: Instruments and observing systems
text:
Epistemic purpose
Drafted human-editable specification · v0.4.4 · no agent-performance claim

title: Instruments and observing systems
text: Expand what can be measured reliably and thereby enable scientific questions.

title: Instruments and observing systems
text:
When this mode helps

A sensor, platform, network, or measurement chain changes the available observations. A software component may be part of that chain.

title: Instruments and observing systems
text:
Agent actions and representations

Specify the target observable; model response; calibrate; compare an independent chain; diagnose artifacts; document deployment and sampling constraints.
Inputs: the question, available evidence and provenance, constraints, prior claims, and remaining budget.
Outputs: inspectable artifacts, updated question/evidence state, and a claim record when a substantive claim is made.

title: Instruments and observing systems
text:
Evidence and claim scope

Show capability over a specified range with response, uncertainty, and failure conditions. Independent-looking instruments can share systematic errors; agreement alone is insufficient.
Distinguish a warranted decision at the time from a claim’s later assessed adequacy; append follow-up without rewriting the original record.

title: Instruments and observing systems
text:
Transitions and stopping

Return to observation after characterizing the chain; use estimation for latent quantities; enter methods for a new extraction procedure and robustness for transfer.
Neighbouring profiles: observation, estimation, methods, robustness.

title: Instruments and observing systems
text:
Characteristic failure

Read instrument response as a physical phenomenon; generalize a capability demonstration beyond the tested conditions; count a device without scientific relevance as advance.

title: Instruments and observing systems
text:
Human evidence and borrowing

Lindsey et al. (2019) and Lindsey et al. (2020) supply a sensing/calibration pair. Tal (2013) and Chang (2004) inform measurement and revisable standards; this is design motivation, not proof of an agent rule.
Cross-field comparison: Chang’s measurement history provides a comparison for revising standards together with instruments; its lesson is not simply to demand two agreeing sensors.
Science of process/impact: Becker et al. (2019) is an infrastructure retrospective, not a causal estimate of instrument investment. Record enabling dependencies rather than crediting every later result to one device.
Definition and evidence (modes meeting, drafted October 2026): Defined as distinct work by Baird (2004); experimentation and invention have “a life of its own” in Hacking (1983) (pp. 150, 163); instruments move between technical and epistemic status (Rheinberger 2011). A new instrument, archive, or computer was a precondition in 15 of 18 coded geoscience advances; a cost shock to one sensing tool widened the knowledge teams combined (Teodoridis 2018). On graph v0.4: N (new capability).
The actions and transitions above are design hypotheses derived from these sources, not established optimal policies. Missing process chronology remains unknown.

title: Instruments and observing systems
text:
Evaluation against past work

Demonstrate a new reliable measurement capability and one relevant question it enables. Test a response change that mimics a new physical signal, and a genuine capability extension.
Use the historical evaluation to choose a source record, preserve evidence boundaries, and assess a meaningful gain. A synthetic control tests a constructed case, not a historical discovery.
Assessment definitions · Agent implementation

title: Methods and computation
text:
Epistemic purpose
Drafted human-editable specification · v0.4.3 · no agent-performance claim

title: Methods and computation
text: Expand what can be inferred or computed with an inspectable method.

title: Methods and computation
text:
When this mode helps

The contribution is an algorithm, representation, or computational procedure; using an established method for a new estimate also invokes estimation.

title: Methods and computation
text:
Agent actions and representations

Specify inputs and assumptions; implement or adapt a method; test known cases and failure conditions; compare baselines; preserve reproducible artifacts and costs.
Inputs: the question, available evidence and provenance, constraints, prior claims, and remaining budget.
Outputs: inspectable artifacts, updated question/evidence state, and a claim record when a substantive claim is made.

title: Methods and computation
text:
Evidence and claim scope

Demonstrate recovery or performance on cases appropriate to the claim, separate development from evaluation, and account for relevant uncertainty and costs. Adoption alone is not correctness.
Distinguish a warranted decision at the time from a claim’s later assessed adequacy; append follow-up without rewriting the original record.

title: Methods and computation
text:
Transitions and stopping

Enter estimation or observation when applying the method; use robustness for transfer; reframe the problem if the method solves the wrong target.
Neighbouring profiles: estimation, observation, robustness, exploration.

title: Methods and computation
text:
Characteristic failure

Leakage produces apparent performance; synthetic recovery is presented as real-world validity; a new implementation adds no useful capability.

title: Methods and computation
text:
Human evidence and borrowing

Shapiro and Campillo (2004) and Shapiro et al. (2005) are geoscience method/application cases. Kapoor and Narayanan (2023) discusses leakage in science; Flake and Fried (2020) motivates checking what a score measures.
Cross-field comparison: Langley (1981) and Kulkarni and Simon (1988) provide historical discovery-system comparisons; their restricted tasks do not establish general scientific autonomy.
Science of process/impact: Chen et al. (2025) evaluates executable scientific tasks and costs. Task completion is evidence of capability, requiring further assessment to establish advance.
Definition and evidence (modes meeting, drafted October 2026): No source defines method development as a mode with its own warrant; the nearest is Hacking’s algorismic style (Hacking 2002). Methods dominate the extreme citation tail (Wren 2016) and new methods are more disruptive (Leahey et al. (2023), abstract). Methods are the core loop of 7 of 19 published agent systems. On graph v0.4: N (new capability) and I (estimate).
The actions and transitions above are design hypotheses derived from these sources, not established optimal policies. Missing process chronology remains unknown.

title: Methods and computation
text:
Evaluation against past work

Show a relevant capability gain against the prior method at comparable cost or explain the tradeoff. Include a data-leakage trap and an out-of-domain failure.
Use the historical evaluation to choose a source record, preserve evidence boundaries, and assess a meaningful gain. A synthetic control tests a constructed case, not a historical discovery.
Assessment definitions · Agent implementation

title: Cross-study synthesis
text:
Epistemic purpose
Drafted human-editable specification · v0.5.0 · split from “Synthesis and reconstruction” on October 21, 2026 · no agent-performance claim

title: Cross-study synthesis
text: Integrate results from many studies or data sets into a pooled estimate, a reconciled account, or a connection between literatures that no single study supports.

title: Cross-study synthesis
text:
When this mode helps

Several studies measure the same quantity with different methods, sites, or teams, and disagree or are too small alone; or two literatures address one problem without citing each other.
Not this mode: reconstructing one past event from its physical traces, which is reconstruction from traces.

title: Cross-study synthesis
text:
Agent actions and representations

State the inclusion rule before searching; record every study screened and why it was kept or dropped; extract effect sizes or estimates with their uncertainties; model dependence between studies (shared data, shared teams, shared methods); test heterogeneity; report the pooled result with its spread.
Inputs: the question, the inclusion rule, the study records and their provenance, the budget.
Outputs: the study table, the dependence structure, the pooled estimate or connection, and a claim record.

title: Cross-study synthesis
text:
Evidence and claim scope

The pooled claim holds only for the population of studies the rule admitted. Dependent studies count once. A literature connection is a hypothesis until a test supports it.
Distinguish a warranted decision at the time from a claim’s later assessed adequacy; append follow-up without rewriting the original record.

title: Cross-study synthesis
text:
Transitions and stopping

Stop when the pooled estimate is stable to the inclusion of any single study and the dependence structure is stated. Hand disagreements to hypothesis assessment; hand pooled quantities to estimation when a forward model is needed; hand a connection to theory for a mechanism.
On graph v0.4.2: a composition, many O records compared at C and combined at K. In the decision tree, question 3 (aim: a pooled estimate) and question 7 (agreement across independent data and methods).

title: Cross-study synthesis
text:
Characteristic failure

Count dependent studies as independent; let the inclusion rule drift after seeing results; pool incompatible quantities; mistake a plausible literature connection for a tested result.

title: Cross-study synthesis
text:
Human evidence and borrowing

Defined for ecology and evolution by the meta-analysis literature (Gurevitch et al. 2018) and organized in synthesis centres (Carpenter et al. 2009). Synthesis-centre papers drew 82.7 against 42.9 mean citations (Hackett et al. 2021).
Geoscience cases: a reference Earth model fitted to many data types at once (Dziewonski and Anderson 1981); a reconciled ice-sheet mass balance across altimetry, gravimetry, and input-output methods (Shepherd et al. 2012); four decades of Antarctic mass balance (Rignot et al. 2019).
Connecting separate literatures: Swanson (1986) motivates literature-based discovery; Nersessian (2022) compares integration processes. One agent system’s synthesis statements were 57.9% accurate against 85.5% for its data analyses (Mitchener et al. 2025).
The actions above are design hypotheses derived from these sources, not established optimal policies.

title: Cross-study synthesis
text:
Evaluation against past work

Reproduce a published synthesis from its study list: same pooled value within its stated spread, and the same verdict when one study is removed. Include a planted dependent pair and a study that fails the inclusion rule.

title: Reconstruction from traces
text:
Epistemic purpose
Drafted human-editable specification · v0.1.0 · split from “Synthesis and reconstruction” on October 21, 2026 · no agent-performance claim

title: Reconstruction from traces
text: Establish what happened in a past event or history, and when, from the physical traces it left, by finding the account that independent traces support and rival histories do not.

title: Reconstruction from traces
text:
When this mode helps

The event is unique and cannot be rerun: a past earthquake, an impact, an ice-sheet retreat. Conditions are found, not set. Reconstruction can still involve new sampling, coring, or experiments on the traces.

title: Reconstruction from traces
text:
Agent actions and representations

List rival histories before reading the traces as support for one; record each trace’s provenance and preservation; judge which traces are independent (different processes, different measurement chains); look for the trace that discriminates between rivals, Cleland’s “smoking gun”; date the events through estimation.
Inputs: the question, the traces and their provenance, the rival histories, dating constraints, the budget.
Outputs: a trace table with independence judged, the rival histories with what each predicts, the retained history with its status, and a claim record.

title: Reconstruction from traces
text:
Evidence and claim scope

A history is retained as the best explanation among the stated rivals, supported by traces that are independent of each other; it is not confirmed by repetition. An event may be unique while its traces admit independent checks.
Distinguish a warranted decision at the time from a claim’s later assessed adequacy; append follow-up without rewriting the original record.

title: Reconstruction from traces
text:
Transitions and stopping

Stop when independent traces converge on one history and the remaining rivals are excluded or stated. Use estimation for dates and magnitudes; hypothesis assessment for rival histories; return to exploration when no rival accounts for the traces.
On graph v0.4.2: the trace-series composition, conditions found at F, O over independent traces in place of V, a best explanation at K. In the decision tree, question 6b when nature does not repeat the event.

title: Reconstruction from traces
text:
Characteristic failure

Treat correlated traces as independent; replace primary records with retellings; read chronology from the order of articles; keep one history without naming its rivals.

title: Reconstruction from traces
text:
Human evidence and borrowing

Defined philosophically by Cleland’s account of historical science, the asymmetry of overdetermination and the search for a smoking gun (Cleland 2001, 2002), and by Turner’s analysis of how prehistory is made from traces (Turner 2007).
Geoscience cases: Cascadia’s great earthquakes from buried marsh soils and turbidites (Atwater 1987; Nelson et al. 1996); the end-Cretaceous impact from the iridium anomaly and the Chicxulub crater (Alvarez et al. 1980; Hildebrand et al. 1991; Schulte et al. 2010).
The actions above are design hypotheses derived from these sources, not established optimal policies. Missing process chronology remains unknown.

title: Reconstruction from traces
text:
Evaluation against past work

Given the traces available at a past date, retain the history the field later accepted, name its rivals, and identify which trace discriminated. Include correlated traces planted as independent and a plausible rival history.
Assessment definitions · Agent implementation

title: Replication and robustness assessment
text:
Epistemic purpose
Drafted human-editable specification · v0.4.4 · no agent-performance claim

title: Replication and robustness assessment
text: Establish what survives repetition, perturbation, or transfer, and correct consequential errors.

title: Replication and robustness assessment
text:
When this mode helps

The question concerns reliability, domain of applicability, or a challenged result. Informative failures can advance knowledge.

title: Replication and robustness assessment
text:
Agent actions and representations

Reproduce analyses; change relevant assumptions; use independent observations; test transfer; localize disagreement; update claim scope and preserve earlier assessments.
Inputs: the question, available evidence and provenance, constraints, prior claims, and remaining budget.
Outputs: inspectable artifacts, updated question/evidence state, and a claim record when a substantive claim is made.

title: Replication and robustness assessment
text:
Evidence and claim scope

State what was repeated and what was independent, with sensitivity, uncertainty, and conditions of failure. Reproducible code alone does not establish empirical adequacy.
Distinguish a warranted decision at the time from a claim’s later assessed adequacy; append follow-up without rewriting the original record.

title: Replication and robustness assessment
text:
Transitions and stopping

Return to the originating mode with revised scope; obtain better observations when disagreement is unresolvable; reframe after a consequential correction.
Neighbouring profiles: instruments, methods, estimation, hypothesis.

title: Replication and robustness assessment
text:
Characteristic failure

Treat agreement as proof; repeat a shared bias; call every difference a refutation; dismiss replication as unoriginal.

title: Replication and robustness assessment
text:
Human evidence and borrowing

Lindsey et al. (2020) supplies measurement assessment; Beven and Freer (2001) motivates sensitivity to equifinality. Nosek et al. (2018) separates planned and unplanned analyses; it does not ban exploratory actions.
Cross-field comparison: Leeman et al. (2024) supplies a materials-science reanalysis, whose conclusions should be attributed and compared with original evidence; it is not a blanket verdict on laboratory agents.
Science of process/impact: Petersen et al. (2025) challenges interpretation of an impact indicator. Flake and Fried (2020) explains why measurement validity needs attention beyond a repeatable score.
Definition and evidence (modes meeting, drafted October 2026): Replication is defined for experiments (Schmidt 2009; Machery 2020) and robustness as agreement across models or means (Wimsatt 2012; Parker 2011); for a one-off natural event the nearest is conceptual replication, a test of the hypothesis “with different methods” (Schmidt 2009, 91). Nonreplicable papers are cited more (Serra-Garcia and Gneezy 2021). In coded geoscience advances, robustness came from converging independent traces (Cleland 2002); for climate models, robustness across models is variety-of-evidence reasoning (Lloyd 2010). On graph v0.4: V (replicate and control).
The actions and transitions above are design hypotheses derived from these sources, not established optimal policies. Missing process chronology remains unknown.

title: Replication and robustness assessment
text:
Evaluation against past work

Demonstrate a corrected conclusion, narrower domain, or meaningful independent support. Include shared systematic errors and a legitimate failure to transfer.
Use the historical evaluation to choose a source record, preserve evidence boundaries, and assess a meaningful gain. A synthetic control tests a constructed case, not a historical discovery.
Assessment definitions · Agent implementation
