No Nature or Science paper fails by citations. Of the 1,717 Earth-science research articles in the two journals from 2005 to 2015, none sits below its field’s median normalized citation; the median is the 99.4th percentile, and 34 (2%) are below the 90th. Stratum D is low only against its journal: 73 to 118 citations is the cut-off.
Failure, as now defined, is not visible in these strata. Failure means no conclusion reached; a contradicted claim is a successful result (convenor, October 21, 2026). Every published paper in C and D reports a conclusion, so neither stratum contains a failure. Later contradictions of Davis et al. (2006) and Wookey and Helffrich (2008) would make them successes of the field, not failures of the papers. A failure corpus has to come from work that ended without a conclusion: conference abstracts never followed by a paper, funded projects without publications, registered reports with inconclusive results.
Highly cited is not broad. The median share of citers outside geoscience is 4% for stratum C, the same as the matched controls with 30 or more citers (4%), and 7% for stratum D. The recognized four reach about 12%, carried by Lam and Rodell. Breadth of uptake does not follow citation success.
The citation tail is products. Among the most-cited Earth-science items, reanalyses, calibration curves, and assessment reports come first (ERA5: 31,639 citations); in 2019 to 2023 the first research article ranks seventh. Seven of the ten C papers contribute a method or an instrument.
Caveats. 366 topics that appear among these papers’ citers were not in the audited map and default to outside, which raises the outside shares. Stratum D’s five-year counts are mostly below 30. None of the 20 has been coded by mode yet; 2 have legal open full texts in hand, 2 more are free on the publisher site, 16 are paywalled.

What the eight show about modes

None entered from a hypothesis. Four entered from a capability, three from a problem, one from an anomaly in a repeat survey.
Node I (estimate a latent quantity) appears in 7 of 8; node N (new capability) in 6; node E (explore) in 6. Node D, designing a discriminating observation before the data, appears once (Lam’s verification design).
Rivals were stated in six papers and excluded by a test in four, one of them only partly. Xu and colleagues list eight possible mechanisms and exclude none; the retained account combines several (p. 479).
Every claim gate was met at least in part; no action gate was. On these eight, the claim gate describes the practice and the action gate does not.
The protective move at P appears three times: Vine and Matthews’s auxiliaries (p. 949), Normandeau and colleagues’ multi-year ice to close a 0.05 m versus 0.2 m gap (p. 10), and Xu and colleagues’ added assumption after a failed length prediction (p. 479).
Interdisciplinary content does not predict interdisciplinary uptake: Xu and colleagues import fracture mechanics, laboratory rupture experiments, and satellite radar, and 4% of their citers are outside geoscience.
None of the recognized four uses the word “first” for its claim; three of the four designated papers do. With eight papers this is a description, not a pattern.

Reproduction, extension

Before deployment on August 6, 2023: lay the cable parallel to the front and run both sensing modes (p. 2)
The process chain and a melt of at most 1 cm per cycle

Reproduction
Correct the borehole pressure records for drift, convert to strain, test locking (pp. 4–9)
Table 1 strain rates; data and code stated to be with the paper (p. 12)
Seafloor drift rates in the text, +0.52, +0.14, and +0.43 kPa/yr (p. 9), differ from Fig. 2 and Table 1, 0.42, 0.13, and 0.39 kPa/yr (pp. 2, 4)
Recent, April 2026

Decision reconstruction, extension
Between March 28 and April 28, 2025: test supershear with independent observables
Supershear at about 5 km/s over about 450 km in the south; cross-fault Vs of 2.9 against 3.3 km/s as a held-out check (p. 477)
The fault-parallel motion test is not unique (p. 478); the mechanism combines eight options, none excluded
Recent; an EarthArXiv preprint exists




Exposure. The four recognized papers are in any model’s training data: use them for reproduction and extension, not blind decision reconstruction. The four designated papers postdate some models’ training; check each model’s training cutoff and whether it can recall the result before using them for decision reconstruction.
Errors in the text are a separate item from planted flaws. An agent that reproduces a result should also flag the Turner-angle sign and the survey date. A model that has memorized the paper may repeat them.

section: What this page does not establish
text:
What this page does not establish

That these eight are advances by any measure other than the convenor’s judgment and, for four of them, citations.
That the metrics discriminate advances: three controls per paper is a start, not a test with power, and the recognized four were chosen on the measure that separates them best. The designated four are the test; their citations mean something only after a few years.
That the codings are reliable: one coder per paper, from the text alone. Two independent codings of a subset would give an agreement figure.

Open the evaluation page. Look up a paper by DOI or open its PDF from your computer (the file stays in your browser and is never uploaded). Then record where the work starts, which of the thirteen modes it uses, the order in which they ran, and how it answered each question of the decision tree. Each answer takes a quote and a page; with the PDF open, the page checks that the quote is on that page.
Your answers stay with you. The page sends nothing. It saves a draft in your browser and downloads your answers as one JSON file; email that file to mdenolle@uw.edu. The questions are generated from the same codebook the coding agent uses, so human and model answers can be compared field by field.

title: What review changes, and what the paper says
text:
Corpus
Drafted v0.3 · October 27, 2026 · round 1, 58 open-review papers · paper codebook 1.5.0 · model-coded and model-labelled, no human check yet
crumbs: What review changes, and what the paper says

title: What review changes, and what the paper says
text:
Source. Round 1 of the roadmap corpus: 525 eligible 2022 papers, 233 coded from full text (see workflows and outcomes and topics and journals).
Copernicus journals. 64 of the 233 are in journals published by Copernicus (DOI prefix 10.5194). All but two are journals of the European Geosciences Union (EGU); European Journal of Mineralogy and Scientific Drilling are published by Copernicus for other societies and have no open discussion, which is why 3 of the 64 have none. 61 have an open discussion; 58 have a review sequence that passed the format check.
Open discussion. In EGU journals the submitted manuscript is posted as a citable discussion preprint. Referee comments, author replies, community comments and editor comments are posted beside it, and the revised paper is published separately and links back to it (Pöschl 2012). The record works like OpenReview for geoscience. Across the 61: 134 referee comments, 147 author comments, 6 community comments and 4 editor comments.
Journals. The Cryosphere (ice and snow) 33; Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences (NHESS, hazards), Geoscientific Model Development (GMD, model code), Hydrology and Earth System Sciences (HESS, hydrology) and Biogeosciences (ecosystems and biogeochemistry) 4 each; Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics (ACP) 3; Earth Surface Dynamics (ESurf, landforms) and Earth System Science Data (ESSD, data sets) 2 each; Geoscientific Instrumentation (GI) and Solid Earth 1 each. The result mostly describes one journal.
crumbs: What review changes, and what the paper says

title: What review changes, and what the paper says
text:
Method

Coding. Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic’s asynchronous batch mode, effort high, no temperature set) read the published paper (PDF and publisher XML text) and the open discussion, and wrote the review process as a sequence of steps on the graph of inquiry. A node is the kind of move (15 types, for example V vary or replicate); a mode is the style of inquiry the step serves (13 types); both are defined on workflows and outcomes. Each step has a node, a mode, an action, a location in the review record, a quote of at most 25 words, a move (forced by review, declined, return after failure) and a trigger (referee, editor, commenter, author). $26.76 for 58 papers.
What the coder read. The discussion comments (referee, author, community and editor) with the supplements attached to them. The tracked-changes manuscripts, author-response PDFs and manuscript versions were downloaded for all 58 papers but not given to the coder, and neither was the article’s own supplement. Because the coder also read the final paper, it may have phrased steps from the final text, which would favour “as if planned” over “not in the paper”.
Labelling. Two model labelers, separate runs of a Claude model inside the Claude Code tool (model id not recorded), each put every step in one of four classes without seeing the other’s labels. A third run settled disagreements. Coder, labelers and adjudicator are all Claude models, so their errors may be correlated.








Label
Rule




Marked as a revision
In the paper, and the paper ties it to review. A generic thank-you to referees does not count.


As if planned
In the paper, with no sign it came from review.


Not in the paper
A change described in review that the published paper does not contain.


No change
A declined request or a reply that only argues.




What the labelers searched. The publisher XML text of the final paper. Its converter keeps body text and captions; only 12 of the 58 texts include an acknowledgements section, and none includes the supplement. A change moved to the supplement would be labelled “not in the paper”.
Checks. Every “in the paper” label carries a quote from the published text, matched by script against that text. Papers, not steps, are the unit for intervals.
crumbs: What review changes, and what the paper says

title: What review changes, and what the paper says
text:
Results



Review steps and their visibility in the published paper (a), share of changes absent by graph node (b), and changes per paper (c). Round 1, 58 open-review papers.



Papers marking any review change: 0 of 58. One-sided 95% upper bound: 5.2% of papers.
Independent check by script. In the published PDFs, 53 of 58 papers mention reviewers or referees, every time in a thank-you or in the journal’s review statement; none uses a phrase that ties content to review (“as suggested by the reviewer”, “in the revised manuscript”, and similar). The labelers’ XML texts contain no mention at all, because most back matter is missing from them. The zero therefore holds on the full PDF text, for the phrases searched.
Not in the paper: 20 of 580 changes, 3.4% (95% interval 1.7% to 5.6%, bootstrap over papers); 13 of 58 papers have at least one. The article supplements were not checked, so some of these may sit there.
What goes missing: V changes (sensitivity tests, comparisons with independent data or methods, controls, reruns) are the most common request and the most often missing: 13 of 102 not in the paper, against 7 of 478 for all other nodes. The 13 absences fall in 10 papers. With papers as units (absences shuffled within each paper, Benjamini-Hochberg over 14 nodes), V exceeds the other nodes by 11 percentage points (interval 4 to 20, q = 0.003); no other node differs. Exploratory: V was singled out after looking.
Who asked: 729 of 746 steps were triggered by referees, 15 by community commenters, 2 by the authors, none coded as triggered by the editor. All 20 absences follow referee requests.
Refusals that still changed the paper: 60 of 220 declined requests left a trace in the published text, usually a caveat or a justification.
Labeler agreement: 720 of 746 steps (96.5%) before adjudication; Cohen’s kappa 0.91 (agreement corrected for chance, see Measures).
Quote existence: 560 of 560 quotes are found verbatim in the published text. This shows the quotes exist, not that each shows the change its label claims; no entailment check (does the quote support the label?) has been run. 44 of the 560 quotes exceed the 25-word limit the labelers were given (7.9%), an instruction-following failure.
October 21 loop pilot, 9 papers with review files (Nature peer-review files, EGU discussions, one preprint revision; a different pilot from the 10-paper labelling pilot of this experiment): 4 of 126 loops readable as loops, 70 as if planned, 52 absent. Same direction. The larger absent share probably reflects construction: the pilot counted analyses discussed in review files that never entered any version.
crumbs: What review changes, and what the paper says

title: What review changes, and what the paper says
text:
Reading the result

For geoscientists. A convention, not misconduct. EGU journals put the whole discussion on the record, on a citable discussion preprint that the final paper links to (Pöschl 2012); the history exists, just not in the paper. Unless the journal publishes review files, readers of closed-review journals have no such record; some closed-review journals do publish them after acceptance (Nature Communications, for example).
For NLP researchers. A loop designed from methods sections sees no review loop. V is among the steps the coded agent loops rarely run: 10% of 31 agent systems against 97% of papers, with Q (question) also at 10% and I (infer) at 5%, H (hypothesize) at 6% and P (protect) at 0%. Refinement (R) goes the other way: agent loops run it more often than papers (68% against 56%). The 31 systems were hand-picked for a comparison talk (14 science agents, 8 general agent patterns, 3 multi-agent, 3 coding, 2 deep-research systems, 1 workflow pattern), coded from their papers and documentation under a separate loop codebook (0.1.2) by two model coders, a Claude Opus run and a Claude Sonnet run. The comparison is between descriptions, not executed runs.
The 31 agent systems. ReAct; Reflexion; Self-Refine; Plan-and-Solve; Tree of Thoughts; LATS; Voyager; BabyAGI; AutoGen, CAMEL and ChatDev (one entry); MetaGPT; Magentic-One; the evaluator-optimizer pattern; coding harnesses (Claude Code, OpenAI SDK); SWE-agent; OpenHands; deep research (OpenAI, Gemini); STORM; Agent Laboratory; Kosmos; Biomni; Virtual Lab; data-to-paper; AIDE; DiscoveryWorld Hypothesizer; Robot Scientist (Adam); Coscientist; Co-Scientist; Robin; The AI Scientist; FunSearch and AlphaEvolve (one entry); Bayesian adaptive design.




Node use in 233 coded papers against 31 AI agent systems (a), distinct nodes per workflow (b), and common researcher transitions that no agent loop runs (c).
crumbs: What review changes, and what the paper says

title: What review changes, and what the paper says
text:
Measures

Review step. One change or refusal recorded in the open discussion, coded as one node on the graph of inquiry.
Change to the work. A review step with any label other than “no change”; the denominator for all shares.
Absent share. Changes labelled “not in the paper” divided by changes; interval is the 2.5 and 97.5 percentiles of 5000 bootstrap resamples of papers.
Upper bound on marking. With 0 of n papers marking a change, the one-sided 95% upper bound on the rate is about 3/n, the rule of three (Hanley and Lippman-Hand 1983).
Per-node share interval (panel b). Wilson 95% interval (Wilson 1927), steps treated as independent, not adjusted for the 14 comparisons. The paper-level test above replaces it for V.
Labeler agreement. Share of steps where the two labelers gave the same label before adjudication.
Cohen’s kappa. Agreement between the two labelers corrected for the agreement expected by chance from each labeler’s label frequencies; 1 is perfect, 0 is chance.
Quote existence. Share of “in the paper” labels whose quote is found verbatim in the normalized published text.
Agent node share. Share of 31 AI agent systems whose loop (the cycle of steps the system repeats) runs a node, mean of the two model coders (loop codebook 0.1.2).
BH q. Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995); defined on workflows and outcomes.
crumbs: What review changes, and what the paper says

title: What review changes, and what the paper says
text:
Limits

Coding, labelling and adjudication by Claude models; agreement between runs of one model family shows stability, not correctness, and errors shared by the runs do not show. No human check and no model from another family yet.
The coder read the final paper as well as the review record, which can only raise “as if planned”. An ablation that codes the review sequence from the review record alone has not been run.
The labelers searched the publisher XML text, which lacks most acknowledgements and every supplement. The PDF string check covers acknowledgements for the phrases searched; supplements remain unchecked.
No recall test: the labelers have not been shown papers with known revision markings, so their ability to find one is assumed, not measured.
Possible contamination: the papers (2022) and their public discussions predate the model’s knowledge cutoff (June 2026), so the model may recall them.
58 papers, one year, 33 from The Cryosphere, all open discussion. Closed-review journals may differ in either direction.
Strict rule for “marked”: generic acknowledgements not counted.
Three papers dropped at the format check: two for quotes over 25 words, one for a schema error.
crumbs: What review changes, and what the paper says

title: What review changes, and what the paper says
text:
Reproduce

Code (this repository): tools/code_papers.py, tools/roadmap/g15_open_review.py, tools/roadmap/g16_visibility.py, tools/roadmap/workflows/visibility.js, codebook agents/coder/ 1.5.0; the string check, trigger counts and paper-level node test in tools/roadmap/g19_report_numbers.py; figures tools/roadmap/figures/fig06_agents.py, fig07_review.py.
Data and codings: data/roadmap-release/, data/roadmap/derived/review/ (open-review index, visibility labels and results) and analysis/codings/api/calc1-review/. The review texts themselves are not included.





Benjamini, Yoav, and Yosef Hochberg. 1995. “Controlling the false discovery rate: A practical and powerful approach to multiple testing.” Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B (Methodological) 57 (1): 289–300. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2517-6161.1995.tb02031.x.


Hanley, James A., and Abby Lippman-Hand. 1983. “If nothing goes wrong, is everything all right? Interpreting zero numerators.” JAMA 249 (13): 1743. https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.1983.03330370053031.


Pöschl, Ulrich. 2012. “Multi-stage open peer review: Scientific evaluation integrating the strengths of traditional peer review with the virtues of transparency and self-regulation.” Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience 6: 33. https://doi.org/10.3389/fncom.2012.00033.


Wilson, Edwin B. 1927. “Probable inference, the law of succession, and statistical inference.” Journal of the American Statistical Association 22 (158): 209–12. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1927.10502953.

title: Research workflows and their outcomes
text:
Measures
Drafted v0.3 · October 27, 2026 · round 1, 233 coded papers · paper codebook 1.5.0 · model-coded, no human check yet · exploratory
Terms used on this page, on topics and journals and on what review changes. The graph itself is on the unit of analysis.
What is coded
Outcomes
Statistics

title: Research workflows and their outcomes
text:
Node. One of 15 kinds of move on the graph of inquiry: N new capability (build or characterize an instrument or method), E explore (establish that a phenomenon is real), O observe, I infer a latent quantity through a forward model (an inverse problem), Q question, H hypothesize rivals, S simulate or derive expectations, D design the test, F find or set the conditions, C compare, V vary or replicate (sensitivity tests, comparisons with independent data or methods, controls, reruns), X exclude a rival, K keep the claim, P protect the claim by revising an auxiliary assumption, R refine.
Mode. One of 13 styles of inquiry that a step serves: observation, exploration, question, hypothesis (testing among rivals), theory (consequences from first principles), simulation (model forecasts or consequences), instruments (building or characterizing an apparatus), methods (a new inference or computational capability), synthesis (combining results across studies), reconstruction (a past event from its traces, as in paleoclimate or past earthquakes), robustness (varying conditions to see whether a result holds), estimation (a latent quantity with its uncertainty), regularities (an empirical relation with its range).
Walk. The coded sequence of steps in the published paper, each step a node with a mode.
Steps. Number of steps in the walk as coded; consecutive steps on the same node count separately (median 22; merging them gives a median of 20).
Revisits. Steps whose node already occurred earlier in the walk. A consecutive repeat counts, so revisits overlap with steps: 15% of revisits are consecutive repeats.
Decisive mode. The mode of the single step without which the paper’s main claim would not exist. “Decided by simulation” means that step is in the simulation mode.
Entry state. How the paper starts: an anomaly, an unsolved problem, a challenged result, a hypothesis, data without theory, a new capability, or an external goal.
Claim status. What the paper ends with: a confirmed claim, a regularity with its range, an estimate with resolution, a characterized capability, and so on.
Composition. The overall shape of the workflow. “Capability first”: the paper builds a new capability before it poses its question.
Borrowed from other fields. The number of concepts, methods, instruments or data from outside Earth science that the coder lists for the paper (codebook section 6). Fields borrowed from: the number of distinct source fields.
V status and kinds of V check. Each check the paper performs on its own result is coded by kind: reproduction (rerun on the same data), replication (new data), method (a second method), robustness (varied parameters or processing), control (a reference, a synthetic test, a null model), generalization (another region or context). V status is full when the paper performs at least one check other than a plain rerun, partial when its only checks are reruns, and none otherwise. The terms reproduction, replication and generalization follow NASEM (2019); V status counts internal checks and does not mean the result was replicated by others. In round 1, 225 of 233 papers are full and 8 none; the most common kinds are control (203 papers), robustness (148), replication (119) and method (116).
Valid coding. The model’s output passes the format check of tools/check_coding.py: required fields, allowed values, steps numbered in order, quotes of 25 words or fewer. The check says nothing about whether the coding is right. Every n on these pages counts valid codings.



cnp (impact). OpenAlex citation-normalized percentile: the paper’s citation count as a percentile among works of the same OpenAlex subfield, publication year and type, 0 to 1, about four years after publication. The reference set follows the OpenAlex subfield label, so a seismology paper that OpenAlex files under Artificial Intelligence is ranked against AI works (topics and journals). Round 1 was drawn with equal numbers per cnp quintile, so the sample median (0.55) is below the pool median (0.75). 233 papers.
FWCI (impact). Field-weighted citation impact: citations divided by the mean for works of the same subfield, year and type (1 is the world average). Citations are right-skewed, so the median paper sits below 1. 233 papers, median 0.48. cnp and FWCI correlate at 0.99.
novelty_pair (novelty). −log10(1 + number of 2017 to 2021 works whose two leading OpenAlex topics are the same pair as the paper’s). Higher means a rarer pair. Median −3.8, which means about 6,300 earlier works share the pair; the most common pair has about 46,000. With about 4,500 OpenAlex topics, a pair of topics is a coarse unit.
breadth_refs (breadth). Share of the paper’s classified references (those with an OpenAlex topic) that lie outside geoscience. Geoscience is the OpenAlex fields Earth and Planetary Sciences and Environmental Science, plus topics filed elsewhere that a manual audit marked as geoscience (seismology, paleomagnetism, seismic instrumentation, among others). 233 papers, median 0.03.
breadth_citers (breadth). The same share for citing works, papers with at least 10 citers after removing self-citations. 53 papers, median 0.00.
Advance. Blind human rating of the paper’s contribution. Pending.



Spearman rho. Rank correlation between a feature and an outcome, −1 to 1; binary features scored 0/1.
Bootstrap interval. 2.5 and 97.5 percentiles of rho over 2000 resamples of papers. At 233 papers its half-width is about ±0.13 (median over the 196 tests that use all 233 papers; range 0.10 to 0.15).
Permutation p. Share of 5000 shuffles of the outcome giving a correlation at least as large in absolute value. The smallest attainable p is 1/5001.
BH q. Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995); q < 0.1 means at most about 10% of the findings below the threshold are expected to be false. It holds when tests are independent or positively dependent, which is the expected case here. Families: the 245 tests on this page; on topics and journals, 16 coverage tests, 104 workflow tests, 16 outcome tests and 45 stratified tests, each adjusted separately.
Benjamini-Yekutieli q. The same adjustment made valid under any dependence, by multiplying BH q by 6.08 for 245 tests. Used as a sensitivity check.
Partial rho. Feature and outcome ranks each regressed on the rank of reference count; the correlation of the residuals.
Run-to-run consistency (test-retest). The same model codes the same paper twice, independently. It measures stability, not accuracy. It does not cap or estimate agreement with human coders, and errors the model repeats on every run do not show.
Node-set overlap. Jaccard index of the sets of nodes in two codings of one paper: shared nodes over nodes in either.
Krippendorff’s alpha. Agreement between two codings corrected for chance (Krippendorff 2019); 1 is perfect, 0 is chance; 0.667 and 0.8 are the usual thresholds for tentative and firm conclusions. When nearly all papers fall in one class, alpha rests on one or two papers and says little.
Cliff’s delta. Probability that a coded paper scores higher than an uncoded one minus the reverse, −1 to 1 (Cliff 1993).
Wilson interval. A binomial confidence interval that stays inside 0 to 1 for small counts (Wilson 1927).

title: Research workflows and their outcomes
text:
Annotation setup

Coder. claude-opus-5-5 through Anthropic’s asynchronous batch mode (half price), effort setting high, maximum 32,000 output tokens (64,000 for a retry after hitting the limit; no round-1 request needed it), no temperature set (API default), no thinking parameter set. One fixed instruction set: codebook 1.5.0 (public commit 01b7f78) and its JSON schema, 29,568 characters, sha256 9e8d9aad…dfc462. The paper goes in as PDF, plus publisher XML text where it existed at submission (116 of the 233 valid codings; 117 were coded from the PDF alone).
Other model steps. The abstract screen used two model calls per abstract that did not see each other’s answer and a third on disagreements (model id not recorded). The agent-loop comparison used a Claude Opus run and a Claude Sonnet run. Every step uses Claude models; no model from another family has been run.
Dates. Round 1 coded October 25 to 26, 2026; retries October 26.

title: Research workflows and their outcomes
text:
Corpus



Corpus construction: papers at each stage in rounds 1 and 2 (a) and reasons for exclusion at the abstract screen (b).



Pool. 14,223 articles from 2022 in OpenAlex (the open bibliographic index that supplies journals, citations and topic labels), restricted four ways: 16 topics and subfields chosen around the convenor’s (the study’s principal investigator’s) work; publishers with a full-text route (Elsevier, Wiley and AGU, Springer Nature, Copernicus, Science Advances, Seismica, Geophysical Journal International, Seismological Society of America journals); at least 15 references; an Earth-science or multidisciplinary venue. MDPI, Frontiers, Taylor & Francis and others are not in the pool. The results describe this pool, not 2022 Earth science as a whole.
Rings. The core ring is the convenor’s own 8 OpenAlex topics (seismology, seismic waves and imaging, earthquakes and tectonics, seismic sensors, cryosphere, high-pressure geophysics); the broad ring is 8 Earth-science subfields. The core ring is 19% of the pool and half of round 1.
Round 1 preselection. 600 papers, half per ring, equal numbers per cnp quintile, subfields taken in turn. Eligibility: an abstract screen by model calls (no human audit), 525 eligible.
Gold set. A frozen sample of 100 of the 525 eligible papers, stratified by ring and by terciles of impact, novelty and breadth. “Gold” names the sample, not its labels: no human labels exist yet. 51 of the 100 had full text at the first coding and were coded a second time; 50 pairs pass the format check. 40 are assigned to four human coders, two per paper; 0 of 40 coded.
Waiting for coding, round 1. 146 papers with full text and no valid coding: 144 fetched after the first batch and 2 whose coding failed the format check. All 146 were sent in a batch on October 27 that has not returned. 82 are AGU papers and 63 Elsevier.
Waiting for coding, round 2. Two batches (154 and 48 papers) submitted, not returned.




Full-text access by publisher for eligible papers, round 1 (a, b) and round 2 (c, d): PDF, publisher XML, or neither, and the open-access share.



Still without a PDF, round 1. A separate 146 of 525 eligible papers (2 of them have publisher XML): mostly Seismological Society of America journals (44), Pleiades and Allerton English translations of Russian-language journals, distributed by Springer (54; paywalled, no text-and-data-mining route), Geophysical Journal International (28) and other Springer Nature journals (12).
Who is coded. The 233 coded papers lean toward open access (83% against 46% of the uncoded), and 33 come from one journal (The Cryosphere). On citation percentile, topic-pair rarity and breadth of references they do not differ clearly from the uncoded papers.




Who is in the sample: citation percentile (a), topic-pair rarity (b), references outside geoscience (c) and open-access share (d) at each stage, and the coded-minus-uncoded difference as Cliff’s delta (e). Points are papers, without identifiers.

title: Research workflows and their outcomes
section: Run-to-run consistency of the model coder
text:
Run-to-run consistency of the model coder



The same model coding the same 50 papers twice (a, d) and the input-format test on 6 papers (b, c).



Same model, same paper, two runs (50 papers). Node-set overlap 0.86; decisive mode matches in 86% of papers; Krippendorff’s alpha 0.74 for node presence and 0.60 to 0.83 for entry state, claim status, decisive mode and composition. Outcome and V status: both runs agree on all 50 papers, but 49 of 50 fall in one class, so alpha (1.0 as a point estimate, undefined in a third of bootstrap resamples) says little.
The features behind the associations. Counts, rank correlation between the two runs: steps 0.76, revisits 0.76, distinct modes 0.83, kinds of V check 0.85, borrowed from other fields 0.87, fields borrowed from 0.81. Binary features, alpha: decisive methods 1.0, decisive simulation 0.74, uses observation mode 0.73, uses node I 0.74, uses synthesis mode 0.65, capability-first composition 0.63. The last two are below the 0.667 threshold.
Format test (6 papers, earlier codebook 1.4.0, two pipelines). Not comparable with the panel above; shown for the input-format question only.
Human check. None yet. This is the main gap.

title: Research workflows and their outcomes
text:
Associations



Spearman correlation of 49 workflow features with five outcomes (a), the 15 tests with q < 0.1 and their 95% bootstrap intervals (b), and correlations among the outcomes (c).



Impact. Steps, revisits, and a decisive simulation step each correlate about 0.2 with cnp and with FWCI. Revisits counted without consecutive repeats give slightly higher values (0.23 with cnp, 0.24 with FWCI; a sensitivity check outside the 245 tests).
Breadth of references. A decisive method, a capability-first composition (below the reliability threshold, see above) and more kinds of V check correlate positively (about 0.2). More distinct modes, using the synthesis mode (below threshold) and using node I correlate negatively (about −0.2).
Novelty. Only the observation mode passes the threshold (0.21).
Breadth of citers (53 papers): no association passes the threshold.
Outcomes are nearly independent of each other (rank correlations from −0.12 to 0.10 between impact, novelty and breadth), except cnp with FWCI (0.99) and the two breadth measures (0.30).
Paper length check. Longer papers have more steps and more citations. Controlling for reference count, the impact correlations drop but stay positive: steps 0.17, revisits 0.15, decisive simulation 0.19 (with cnp).
A check of the coder, not an outcome result. The count of items borrowed from other fields (0.57 with breadth_refs) and the number of fields borrowed from (0.51) measure the same thing as breadth_refs: one from the text, as the coder reads it, one from the reference list. Their agreement is a convergent validity check of the coder, not a finding about workflows and outcomes.
Stricter correction. Under Benjamini-Yekutieli none of the 245 tests passes (smallest q 0.15), partly because 5000 permutations cannot give p below 0.0002.
Field and venue. All 15 keep their sign and q < 0.1 within subfield and within journal family; within subfield × family, 12 of 15 do. Counting only associations whose bootstrap interval excludes 0, the numbers are 14, 12 and 8 of 15. The impact correlations of steps and revisits roughly halve within journal family (steps with cnp: 0.23 to 0.12). Details on topics and journals.

title: Research workflows and their outcomes
text:
Reading the result

For geoscientists. Work that loops back more and is decided by simulation is cited a little more; about half of that goes with the journal. Work decided by a new method, or that starts from a new capability, cites more outside geoscience; work that combines many modes or synthesizes across studies cites less.
For NLP researchers. Of 245 tests, 15 pass q < 0.1. The two largest (0.57, 0.51) partly restate the reference list; the rest lie between 0.18 and 0.25 in absolute value. With an interval of about ±0.13 on each rho, these can be detected but not ranked against one another. The sample was drawn with equal numbers per cnp quintile, so correlations with cnp describe this design, not the 2022 population; no inverse-probability weighting has been applied.
None of this is causal. Open access, team size and topic differ between papers and are not controlled here; field and venue are checked on topics and journals.
Novelty as measured (a rare topic pair) barely relates to any workflow feature. Either the proxy is weak or novelty does not show in the workflow; the blind human ratings should help separate the two.

title: Research workflows and their outcomes
text:
Limits

One model coder (Claude Opus 5.5) and Claude models at every other step; run-to-run node overlap 0.86 on 50 papers; no human check and no cross-model check yet. A run of an open-weight model (one whose weights are public and can be served locally) through tools/code_papers_open.py on the same 50 papers is prepared but not run.
Possible contamination: the papers are from 2022 and the model’s knowledge cutoff is June 2026, so the papers and their reception are probably in its training data. The coder may draw on memory as well as on the text. Not tested; a probe would code from title and DOI alone and compare.
233 of 525 eligible round-1 papers, open-access-leaning; citations at about four years. Round 2 not yet coded.
Proxies: novelty and breadth are bibliometric stand-ins, not normalized by subfield; advance is missing.
245 tests: by construction about 1 to 2 of the 15 will be false positives at q < 0.1.

title: Topics and journals
text:
Measures
Drafted v0.2 · October 27, 2026 · round 1, 233 coded papers; round 2 drawn, coding not returned · paper codebook 1.5.0 · exploratory
Full definitions of the workflow features (node, mode, steps, revisits, decisive mode), valid coding, Spearman rho, bootstrap intervals and BH q are on workflows and outcomes. The outcome metrics, in brief (all from OpenAlex, retrieved October 2026, about four years after publication):
novelty_pair and breadth_refs are not normalized by subfield, so part of any difference between subfields is field structure.
Terms used only here:

title: Topics and journals
text:
cnp (impact). Citation-normalized percentile: the paper’s citation count ranked among works of the same OpenAlex subfield, year and type, 0 to 1.
FWCI (impact). Field-weighted citation impact: citations divided by the mean for those works; 1 is the world average. cnp and FWCI correlate at 0.99, so they are one impact signal.
novelty_pair (novelty). −log10(1 + number of 2017 to 2021 works whose two leading OpenAlex topics are the same pair as the paper’s); higher means a rarer pair.
breadth_refs (breadth). Share of the paper’s classified references that lie outside geoscience.
Advance. A blind human rating of the contribution; not yet measured, so not used here.




OpenAlex topic, subfield, field. OpenAlex assigns each paper a leading topic by a classifier over title, abstract, venue and citations; topics nest in subfields and fields (for example, the topic Seismic Imaging and Inversion Techniques sits in the subfield Geophysics, which sits in the field Earth and Planetary Sciences). These are machine labels, not author keywords. OpenAlex files topics, not papers, under subfields, so a subfield can hold topics from another discipline.
Ring. Round 1 drew half its papers from the core ring, the convenor’s own 8 OpenAlex topics (seismology, seismic waves and imaging, earthquakes and tectonics, seismic sensors, cryosphere, high-pressure geophysics), and half from the broad ring, 8 Earth-science subfields. The convenor is the study’s principal investigator.
Journal family. Publisher group from DOI prefix, then publisher, then journal name. AGU (American Geophysical Union, the largest US geoscience society) is its own family although Wiley publishes its journals. Copernicus (mostly EGU): journals with DOI prefix 10.5194, nearly all of the European Geosciences Union, plus European Journal of Mineralogy and Scientific Drilling. SSA: Seismological Society of America (Bulletin of the Seismological Society of America, Seismological Research Letters). Oxford: Oxford University Press, here Geophysical Journal International, published for the Royal Astronomical Society. Springer Nature (other) includes English translations of Russian-language journals distributed by Springer (Pleiades, Allerton), which are paywalled and have no text-and-data-mining route.
Effective number of journals. 1/HHI, where the Herfindahl index HHI is the sum of squared journal shares: the number of equal-sized journals with the same concentration.
Cramér’s V. Strength of association between two categorical variables, 0 (independent) to 1 (one determines the other); bias-corrected (Bergsma 2013). Unrelated to node V. Its 95% interval is a percentile interval of the resampled V, which is biased upward under resampling, so read the interval as spread; it can sit above its own estimate.
Rate difference. Share of papers with a property in one category minus the share in all other categories.
Kruskal-Wallis epsilon squared. Kruskal-Wallis H (Kruskal and Wallis 1952), a rank-based one-way analysis of variance, divided by n − 1: the share of rank variance in a count or outcome explained by the grouping, 0 to 1.
Within-stratum rank correlation. Spearman correlation computed after centring both ranks within each subfield (or family, or subfield × family); only co-variation inside a stratum counts. Its p comes from shuffling outcomes within strata.
Holds within strata (“survives”). Same sign as the original correlation and BH q < 0.1 over the 45 stratified tests (15 associations × 3 stratifications). Reported with the stricter count of those whose bootstrap interval also excludes 0.
Test families. BH q is computed separately for the 16 coverage tests, the 104 workflow tests (40 binary features, 9 counts and 3 whole categorical variables, each tested once against subfield and once against journal family), the 16 outcome tests and the 45 stratified tests.

title: Topics and journals
text:
Who is in the corpus



Share of papers by OpenAlex subfield (a) and journal family (b) at each stage of rounds 1 and 2, the most frequent journals among coded papers at three stages (c), and coding rate by journal family relative to all other families (d). Subfield labels name the dominant leading topic where one topic holds at least 60% of the subfield’s coded papers.



Concentration. Effective number of journals falls at each step of round 1: 68 in the pool, 51 preselected, 44 eligible, 40 with full text, 27 coded. Round 2, drawn at most 4 per journal, has 111 effective journals at the draw.
Cryosphere: design, then access. The topic “Cryospheric studies and observations” is 3.9% of the pool. The design raises it to 13.5% of the round-1 preselection, because it is one of the 8 core-ring topics. Access raises it further: 14.9% of eligible, 19% of full-text and 23% of coded papers (53). The Cryosphere, an open-access EGU journal that is fully coded, holds 33 coded papers.
“Artificial Intelligence” is seismology. This OpenAlex subfield is 0.8% of the pool and 11% of the round-1 preselection (64 papers). All 64 have the leading topic “Seismology and Earthquake Studies”, one of the convenor’s core-ring topics, which OpenAlex files under Computer Science. Of the 17 coded, 13 use machine-learning terms somewhere in their coding and 6 build a new capability described in such terms, against 18 of 216 and 4 of 216 in other subfields. They are seismology papers, many of them machine-learning seismology.
Other subfield names. “Atmospheric Science” holds 81 of its 125 preselected papers under the cryosphere topic (72% of its coded papers). “Ocean Engineering” is the seismic-sensor topic “Geophysics and Sensor Technology” (19 of 19). “Space and Planetary Science” is an archaeology topic (4 of 4, none eligible). “Water Science and Technology” mixes hydrology with water-treatment topics. The full topic-to-subfield table is in the data release (data/roadmap/derived/topics/TOPICS.md, section 6).
Access versus timing. Among eligible round-1 papers, journal family predicts reaching a coding strongly (Cramér’s V 0.73), subfield weakly (0.26). Among papers that already have full text, subfield no longer predicts coding (0.12, interval includes 0) while family still does (0.86). AGU and Elsevier papers were fetched after the round-1 batch; 82 AGU and 63 Elsevier papers are in the batch of 146 sent on October 27. SSA, GJI and the translated Russian-language journals are the access gap.

title: Topics and journals
section: Workflows and outcomes by field and venue
text:
Workflows and outcomes by field and venue



Node use and decisive mode by subfield (a), steps, revisits and citation outcomes by journal family (b), and the 15 workflow-outcome associations recomputed within subfield, within journal family, and within both (c).



Workflow differs by subfield. 28 of the 104 workflow tests pass q < 0.1. Earth-surface process papers (mostly geological-formation, aeolian and coastal topics) are decided by reconstruction, inferring a past event from its traces, in 42% of cases against 11% overall. Papers in the seismology group that OpenAlex calls Artificial Intelligence are decided by a method in 76% of cases against 29% overall, and 88% build a new capability (node N).
Walk length differs by venue. Median steps: AGU 24.5 (16 papers), Copernicus 24 (64), Nature portfolio 22.5 (14), Springer Nature other 22 (44), Wiley outside AGU 19.5 (76).
Citations differ by venue. Median cnp among coded papers: AGU 0.80, Copernicus 0.65, Wiley outside AGU 0.43 (epsilon squared 0.13).
AGU is not a sample of AGU. The 16 coded AGU papers are the ones whose text arrived before the first batch; all 16 are open access, against 70 of the 98 eligible AGU papers. The AGU medians, and any venue effect that leans on them, are provisional until the 82 AGU papers now in the batch are coded.
Novelty and breadth differ by subfield (epsilon squared 0.11 and 0.12). The seismology group filed under AI cites outside geoscience most (median 0.27 against 0.03). Neither measure is normalized by subfield, so part of this is field structure.

title: Topics and journals
text:
Confounding check

Breadth and novelty associations hold within field and venue. All 9 keep their sign with q < 0.1 within subfield, within family, and within subfield × family; for two (capability first, observation mode) some stratified intervals include 0. Items borrowed from other fields stay at 0.52 to 0.57 with references outside geoscience, fields borrowed from at 0.48 to 0.52. These two are a convergent validity check of the coder (the same thing measured from the text and from the reference list), not workflow-outcome findings.
Impact associations are partly a venue effect. Within journal family, the correlations of steps and revisits with cnp and FWCI roughly halve (steps with cnp: 0.23 to 0.12). Long walks are more common in AGU and Copernicus journals, which are also cited more. Within subfield they do not change. Provisional, given the AGU sample.
Decisive simulation keeps most of its association with impact in every stratification (0.13 to 0.19).
Three of 15 do not pass within subfield × family: steps with cnp, steps with FWCI, revisits with FWCI.

title: Topics and journals
text:
Caveats

Topic, subfield and field are OpenAlex machine labels. cnp and FWCI are normalized within the OpenAlex subfield, so seismology papers filed under Artificial Intelligence are ranked against AI works and cryosphere papers against atmospheric-science works.
Groups with fewer than 10 coded papers are pooled; Geology (9), Elsevier (9), Oxford (6) and SSA (2) are not compared on their own.
Holding subfield and family fixed does not hold fixed open access, team size or topic within subfield.
Round 2 is not coded yet; its 202 full-text papers are spread over 114 journals and will change the coded composition.
One model coder; citations at about four years.

Bergsma, Wicher. 2013. “A bias-correction for Cramér’s V and Tschuprow’s T.” Journal of the Korean Statistical Society 42 (3): 323–28. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jkss.2012.10.002.


Kruskal, William H., and W. Allen Wallis. 1952. “Use of ranks in one-criterion variance analysis.” Journal of the American Statistical Association 47 (260): 583–621. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1952.10483441.

crumbs: How Earth-science papers describe their research workflows: the roadmap experiments, round 1

title: How Earth-science papers describe their research workflows: the roadmap experiments, round 1
text:
Summary
We asked a large language model to read 2022 Earth-science papers and write down each paper’s research workflow as a walk on a graph. The graph’s vertices (nodes) are fifteen kinds of research move, such as question, observe, infer, compare, and vary and replicate. Each step also carries one of thirteen modes, the style of inquiry it serves (estimation, reconstruction, methods, and so on). The coder is Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5) under codebook 1.5.0; every step of a coding must cite a page or paragraph locator and a quote of at most 25 words. From an OpenAlex pool of 14,223 candidate papers, round 1 preselected 600, kept 525 after an abstract screen, had full text for 235 at the time of coding, and obtained 233 valid codings.
Terms used in the bullets, defined fully in sections 3 to 7: entry state, what started the work as the paper tells it; decisive mode, the mode of the one step without which the main claim would not exist; composition, a named overall pattern of the walk; Krippendorff’s alpha, agreement corrected for chance (1 perfect, 0 chance); q, a p value adjusted for many tests (Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate); rho, Spearman rank correlation; cnp, a citation percentile within the paper’s OpenAlex subfield and year; agent loop, the cycle an AI research system repeats.

The coder agrees with itself on most fields; agreement with human coders is not yet measured. Coding 50 papers twice gave alpha 0.83 for decisive mode (95% bootstrap interval 0.70 to 0.93), 0.77 for entry state (0.50 to 0.95), 0.74 for which nodes a paper uses (0.70 to 0.79) and 0.60 for composition (0.38 to 0.77). Raw agreement on entry state is 92%, but 78% of papers carry its most common label. Outcome and V status (whether the paper checks its own result) cannot be scored this way: 49 of 50 papers fall in one class. Two codings of the same paper overlap more than codings of two different papers, though less than the raw numbers suggest: node-set overlap 0.86 against 0.65 for two different papers.
Most papers share a core of moves. Nearly every paper questions, compares, varies or replicates, and keeps a claim. The median paper has 22 coded steps and returns to modes it has already used. Only 1 of 233 contains the textbook order question, hypothesis, simulate, design, find conditions, observe, compare, even with other steps allowed in between.
Field and venue shape the workflow. 28 of 104 tests of workflow against OpenAlex subfield or journal family have q < 0.1. Seismology papers that OpenAlex files under the subfield Artificial Intelligence are built around a new method, Earth-Surface Processes papers around reconstruction from traces, and AGU and Copernicus papers have longer workflows than the other Wiley journals. The AGU contrast rests on 16 papers that are not a random draw from AGU.
A few workflow features track citations and breadth, and venue explains part of the citation link. 15 of 245 feature-outcome tests have q < 0.1; none passes the stricter Benjamini-Yekutieli correction, which allows any dependence among tests. Longer workflows go with higher citation percentile (rho 0.23; 0.17 with reference count held fixed; 0.12 within journal family). The largest correlation, between the number of items the coder lists as borrowed from other fields and the share of references outside geoscience (rho 0.57), is a check that the coder reads the papers consistently with their reference lists, not an outcome result.
Review changes enter the paper unattributed. Of 580 review-driven changes in 58 Copernicus papers with open discussion (33 in The Cryosphere), 560 read as planned, 20 are absent, and none is marked as a revision.
Published agent designs include few of the moves papers report most often. Against 31 published agent designs, the largest gaps are at question (98% of papers, 10% of agent systems), vary or replicate (97% against 10%), infer (82% against 5%) and hypothesize rivals (81% against 6%). The gaps hold for the 14 research systems alone, and papers and agents were coded from different kinds of text.
The sample is set by full-text access. Coded papers are concentrated in a few venues: The Cryosphere alone is 14% of them, and every eligible Copernicus paper was coded while 16 of 98 AGU papers were. The pending batches should reduce this skew.

Recorded model spend for all experiments to date: $123.59 of a $250 cap; $0.32 per paper for the main coding.

title: How Earth-science papers describe their research workflows: the roadmap experiments, round 1
section: 1. Question, and why it matters to two fields
text:
1. Question, and why it matters to two fields
Two problems motivate the roadmap. Experts reach different conclusions from the same data, and much of the inquiry behind a paper never reaches the paper. The roadmap measures what papers say about how their research was done, and codes it so that human workflows and AI agent loops can be compared on the same graph.
For geoscientists. Much of Earth science works with conditions found in nature rather than set in a laboratory. An earthquake, a glacier or a storm cannot be rerun, so the field relies on reconstruction from traces, on nature repeating itself across events, and on checks such as synthetic tests (running a method on simulated data with a known answer), independent stations or a second inversion method (inversion: estimating unobserved Earth properties from measurements by fitting a physical model). Laboratory work (experimental petrology, rock mechanics, geochemistry) and numerical experiments set their own conditions, and there controls and replication take their usual meaning. Whether published papers show those checks, and whether the shape of a workflow relates to how a paper is cited or how far it reaches outside the field, are questions about the field’s own practice. They can be asked at scale only if reading papers can be automated with known error.
For NLP and AI researchers. Research agents such as The AI Scientist (Lu et al., 2026), Coscientist (Boiko et al., 2023) and the AI co-scientist (Gottweis et al., 2026) are designed and evaluated mostly from what published papers report. If papers present the workflow selectively, agents learn a cleaner process than the one people follow. This study is also an annotation experiment: a large language model (Claude Opus 5.5) as annotator of a long, technical, structured coding task (one JSON object with dozens of fields per paper), with measured test-retest consistency, an input-format ablation (rerunning with one input changed), validation by a deterministic checker (a script, not a model), and cost per document.
Five questions organize the report:

How consistently does the model code workflows (section 4)?
What do Earth-science workflows look like on the graph (section 5)?
Do workflows differ by field and venue (section 6)?
Do workflow features relate to citation, novelty and breadth, and does field or venue explain that (section 7)?
What does the paper leave out: the work done in peer review (section 8) and the moves AI agents skip (section 9)?
crumbs: How Earth-science papers describe their research workflows: the roadmap experiments, round 1

title: How Earth-science papers describe their research workflows: the roadmap experiments, round 1
text:
2. Corpus



Corpus construction


Figure 1. Stages of both rounds and screening exclusions.
Notation. Numbers in square brackets are 95% percentile bootstrap intervals: the statistic recomputed on 2,000 samples of papers drawn with replacement, unless a section says otherwise. q is a p value adjusted by the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure for the number of tests in its family (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995; section 6): among results with q < 0.1, about 10% are expected to be false on average. cnp is the OpenAlex citation normalized percentile, a paper’s citation count as a percentile among works of the same OpenAlex subfield, year and type (0 to 1); the other outcome metrics are defined in section 7.
Pool. We drew from OpenAlex, an open bibliographic index that supplies each paper’s journal, publisher, citation counts and machine-assigned topic labels (Priem et al., 2022). The pool is every 2022 journal article with an abstract and at least 15 references in Earth-science venues that have a full-text route, split into a “core” ring (the eight OpenAlex topics of the convenor, M. Denolle, who runs the seminar and the project) and a “broad” ring (eight neighbouring Earth-science subfields): 14,223 papers (g02_pool.py). Papers with a convenor co-author are excluded from both draws.
Round 1. 600 papers preselected, 300 per ring, with equal numbers per cnp quintile (120 per quintile) and, within a quintile, subfields taken in turn (g03_preselect.py, seed 2026). The design makes the citation distribution near-uniform (sample median cnp 0.55, pool median 0.75) and raises small subfields: the OpenAlex subfield Artificial Intelligence, which in this pool holds only the core-ring topic Seismology and Earthquake Studies, is 0.8% of the pool and 11% of the preselection.
Round 2. 277 open-access papers drawn from the rest of the pool, at most 4 per journal, round robin over publishers (g18_round2_draw.py, seed 2027): 157 journals, 12 publishers.
Screen. Each abstract went to two independent model screeners, with a third model call settling disagreement or uncertainty (16 of 600 adjudicated in round 1, 4 of 277 in round 2). The screeners are Claude agents in a Claude Code workflow (tools/roadmap/workflows/gold-eligibility-screen.js, effort medium); the workflow does not set or record the model version. In NLP terms this is double annotation with adjudication; in a systematic review it is the eligibility step. It drops off-topic papers, reviews, and comments or replies, since the codebook codes research workflows. Round 1 kept 525 of 600 (87.5%; 54 off-topic, 12 reviews, 5 comments or replies, 4 other). Round 2 kept 222 of 277 (80.1%); the screeners agreed on 275 of 277.



Full-text access by publisher


Figure 2. Full text by publisher (PDF, publisher XML) and open-access share.
Full text. The coder needs the whole paper. At the first coding (October 25), 235 of 525 round-1 papers had a PDF. A re-fetch on October 27 from the University of Washington network, with the Wiley route corrected for AGU DOIs, added 192 PDFs across both rounds (144 round 1, 48 round 2; Wiley 106, Elsevier 85, Springer 1) and 103 Elsevier XML files (74 round 1, 29 round 2; refetch_2026-10-27.log). Round 1 now has a PDF for 379 of 525 (72.2%) and text of either kind for 381; round 2 has 202 of 222 (91%), high by design because it was drawn from open-access papers. Round-1 papers still without a PDF are mostly in journals of the Seismological Society of America (SSA: the Bulletin of the Seismological Society of America and Seismological Research Letters, 44), English translations of Russian-language journals that Pleiades (43) and Allerton Press (11) publish and Springer distributes, and Geophysical Journal International (GJI, Oxford University Press, 28). Publisher XML matters for NLP readers because it gives section-and-paragraph locators, so every quote can be found by string search; it exists for 190 round-1 papers now, and 116 of the 233 coded papers were coded with it (section 3).



Who is in the sample


Figure 3. Outcome metrics and open-access share by stage, and the coverage effect.
Who got coded. Full-text access filters the sample. In round 1, 83% of the 233 coded papers are open access, against 46% of the 292 eligible papers not coded, a difference of 37 percentage points [30, 45]. The cnp of coded papers is slightly higher (median difference +0.07 [−0.01, +0.18]). Topic-pair rarity (novelty_pair) and the share of references outside geoscience (breadth_refs) do not differ.



Field and venue by stage


Figure 4. Subfield and journal family at each stage, the most frequent journals, and coverage by family.
Journals and topics. Two groupings are used throughout. Subfield is the OpenAlex subfield of the paper’s leading topic. OpenAlex assigns topics with a classifier over title, abstract, venue and citations; topics nest in subfields (Geophysics, Atmospheric Science, Oceanography) and fields (Earth and Planetary Sciences, Environmental Science). These are machine labels, not author keywords, and the subfield names can mislead:

OpenAlex files the topic Seismology and Earthquake Studies under the subfield Artificial Intelligence, in the field Computer Science. Here that subfield holds only this topic: 17 coded seismology papers, 13 of which have machine-learning (ML) terms somewhere in their coding and 6 in a new-capability step. This report calls it “Seismology (OpenAlex: Artificial Intelligence)”; the figures label it “Artificial intelligence (100% seismology)”.
As coded, Atmospheric Science is 72% the topic Cryospheric studies and observations (53 of 74 papers), that is glaciology and ice sheets rather than meteorology; The Cryosphere alone has 33 coded papers. Earth-Surface Processes is geological formations (12 of 26), aeolian (5) and coastal (5) topics. Water Science and Technology is mostly watershed hydrology (11 of 14). Geophysics is led by seismic imaging and inversion (17 of 64) and earthquake and tectonic studies (14).

Journal family is the publisher group read from the DOI prefix, then the publisher name:

AGU (American Geophysical Union) journals, which Wiley publishes, counted apart from the other Wiley journals;
Wiley non-AGU, led in the coded set by Geophysical Prospecting (13), Geological Journal (9), Basin Research (5), Hydrological Processes (5), Earth Surface Processes and Landforms (4) and Terra Nova (4), mostly applied geophysics, sedimentary geology and hydrology;
Copernicus Publications: the EGU (European Geosciences Union) journals, such as The Cryosphere, Hydrology and Earth System Sciences and Geoscientific Model Development, plus journals Copernicus publishes for other societies, such as European Journal of Mineralogy and Scientific Drilling;
the Nature portfolio (for example Scientific Reports, 8, and Communications Earth & Environment, 4);
the rest of Springer Nature, led by Earth, Planets and Space (13), and including the Pleiades and Allerton translations;
Elsevier; Oxford University Press (mainly GJI); SSA; and AAAS (the American Association for the Advancement of Science, publisher of Science and Science Advances).

For NLP readers: families differ in more than publisher. Their journals differ in length limits, data policies, review process, citation rates and topic, and several families mix society and commercial journals, so venue can stand in for many unmeasured properties of a paper.
The coded set is much more concentrated than the pool. The effective number of journals is 1/HHI, where HHI (the Herfindahl-Hirschman index) is the sum of squared journal shares; it falls from 67.7 in the pool to 51.2 preselected, 43.5 eligible, 39.8 with full text and 27.4 coded, and the top-5 journal share rises from 0.20 to 0.33. The Cryosphere holds 1.7% of the pool, 6.3% of eligible papers and 14.2% of coded papers (33 of 233). The leading topic “Cryospheric studies and observations” goes from 3.9% of the pool to 22.7% of coded papers. Wiley non-AGU (76 papers) and Copernicus (64) make up 60% of coded papers; AGU (16) and Elsevier (9) are under-represented against pool shares of 23.5% and 22.5%.
The skew follows publisher, through download timing, not subfield. Bias-corrected Cramér’s V (the strength of association between two categorical variables, 0 for independence, 1 when one determines the other, corrected for the upward bias of small tables; Bergsma, 2013) is 0.73 between family and being coded, against 0.26 for subfield, among eligible papers. All 64 eligible Copernicus papers are coded, 63 points above the rest. AGU has full text for 98 of 98 but only 16 coded; Elsevier has 72 with full text and 9 coded. Among papers with full text, being coded depends on family (Cramér’s V 0.86) but not on subfield (Cramér’s V 0.12, interval includes 0; q 0.13). The cause is timing: the AGU and Elsevier text arrived in the October 27 re-fetch, after the round-1 batch was submitted. Those papers are most of the 146 in the pending top-up (82 AGU, 63 Elsevier).
Round 2 is more even: 111 effective journals and a top-5 share of 0.07 among the 277 drawn. Its full-text coverage is independent of subfield (q 0.76) but still tied to family (Cramér’s V 0.53, driven by small pooled venues, mainly Seismica, a community-run open-access seismology journal).

text:
4. Self-consistency of the coder (test-retest)



Run-to-run consistency of the model coder


Figure 6. Test-retest agreement, the format test, and Krippendorff’s alpha.
Design (experiment E2). The gold set is a stratified sample of 100 eligible round-1 papers, 50 per ring, spread over terciles of cnp, novelty_pair and breadth_refs (g05_select.py, seed 2026), reserved for human coding. Despite its name it carries no human labels yet; here it serves as the retest sample. The 51 gold papers that had full text at E1 were coded a second time, independently, from the same input (tag gold-r2); 50 pairs passed validation in both runs (one second coding failed the schema). The retest sample resembles the coded set: 41 of 50 entry states are problem (82%, against 78% of all 233), and 16 papers are Copernicus (32%, against 27%), 13 Wiley non-AGU, 9 Springer Nature, 4 Elsevier and 3 AGU. For geoscientists: test-retest asks whether the same instrument gives the same reading twice; inter-annotator agreement asks whether two annotators label the same item the same way. Here instrument and annotator are the same model, sampled at the API’s default temperature, so this is test-retest of a stochastic coder. It shows whether the coder is stable. It says nothing about whether it is right, and it does not cap agreement with a human. A coder that gives the correct label with probability 0.6 and spreads the rest evenly over four wrong labels agrees with itself 40% of the time (0.6² + 4 × 0.1²) but with a human who picks the correct label 60% of the time. Errors the model repeats on every run do not show at all. With two runs per paper, per-item variance cannot be estimated; the next retest should draw 3 to 5 runs on a subset and report how stable the majority label is.
Agreement measures.

Agreement on a categorical field (entry state, outcome, decisive mode): the share of papers with the same value in both codings.
Node-set overlap: the Jaccard index of the sets of nodes used, that is the number of nodes in both codings divided by the number in either. Mode-set overlap is the same for modes.
Sequence similarity: 1 minus the normalized edit distance between the two node (or mode) sequences, after merging consecutive repeats. The edit distance is the number of single-step insertions, deletions and substitutions that turn one sequence into the other; it is divided by the length of the longer sequence (tools/check_coding.py).
Between-paper baseline: the same measure averaged over every pair of two different papers’ codings (27,028 pairs of the 233 calc1 codings). Nearly every paper uses K, C, Q, V and O, so two unrelated papers already overlap. The chance-corrected value is (retest − baseline) / (1 − baseline).
Krippendorff’s alpha (Krippendorff, 2019): agreement corrected for chance, alpha = (observed agreement − chance agreement) / (1 − chance agreement), with chance agreement from how often each category is used. When one category dominates, chance agreement is high and the same raw agreement gives a lower alpha. Common reference points are 0.667 (tentative) and 0.8 (reliable). Node presence alpha treats each paper and node as one unit (is node n used, yes or no). Intervals are bootstrap over papers (Hayes & Krippendorff, 2007).

Results. Entry state agrees in 92% of papers, entry node in 90%, outcome in 100%, decisive mode in 86%. Against the between-paper baseline:

Both acceptance gates passed (node-set overlap at least 0.7; entry and outcome agreement at least 0.8). The roadmap plan fixed these gates before E2 ran (private/analysis/roadmap-plurality-loops.md, Phase 0), but the node-set gate sits only 0.05 above what two different papers give, so passing it says little; a gate on the chance-corrected overlap would be more informative. Alpha is 0.83 for decisive mode [0.70, 0.93], 0.77 for entry state [0.50, 0.95], 0.76 for claim status [0.60, 0.89], 0.74 for node presence [0.70, 0.79] and 0.60 for composition [0.38, 0.77]. Alpha for outcome and V status cannot be estimated: 49 of 50 papers fall in one class (kept, and full), both runs agree on the one exception, and the bootstrap interval is undefined in a third of resamples. The coder is stable on which moves a paper makes and what it concludes, less so on the order of the moves and on which named pattern the walk fits.
What is missing: the human comparison. No human coding has been scored against the model yet, so every number in sections 5 to 9 inherits the coder’s errors, and test-retest cannot detect the systematic ones. The design is fixed in DECISIONS.md (g09_human_coding_app.py): 40 of the 100 gold papers, 20 per ring, spread over impact tiers, each coded independently by two of four lab coders (Marine Denolle, Sangwoo Han, Maleen Kidiwela, Michael Hemmett; six pairs in rotation, 20 papers per coder; seed 2026). The coders see no citation metrics; they code with the earlier codebook 1.3.0, which has no V-check kinds, and rate novelty and advance blind (Novelty Dossier v1, Scientific Advance Profile v1). No coding has been returned. The roadmap plan sets the targets: alpha at least 0.67 on categorical fields (entry state, outcome, node set, mode set) before model coding is trusted, and 0.8 for anything used as an outcome. Not yet decided, and proposed here: score the model against the human consensus on entry state, decisive mode, node presence and claim status; adjudicate human disagreements by discussion; report any field below 0.667 as unreliable and revise the codebook before round 2 is read. The E4 review labels and the 4.1 audit sample are not in the human design yet.

4.1 Entry state: what the label records
Each coded paper carries one of the seven entry states of section 3, and the coder must quote the sentence that supports its choice. In round 1, the model coder labelled 78% of 233 papers as starting from a problem.
That share raised a concern familiar to readers of scientific prose. Most research articles contain a gap statement in the introduction, a sentence such as “the controls on X remain poorly understood”. Swales (1990) described this as the second move of a standard rhetorical pattern: establish the field, point to a gap, then fill it. (Swales’s “move” is rhetorical; it is not a node of our graph.) If the coder quotes that sentence, every paper looks problem-driven, whatever actually set the work going. In NLP terms, the gap sentence is a surface cue the coder can key on in place of the label’s intended meaning.
We tested this with a blind audit. From the round-1 codings we drew 60 papers, stratified by label (36 coded problem, four of each other state; numpy default_rng, seed 2026). Two further coders, A and B, re-coded the entry from the full text without seeing the original label or each other’s work. A and B are Claude agents run in Claude Code, of the same model family as the batch coder (claude-opus-5-5), not people. Besides the entry state, each recorded the operational start, meaning the thing the study could not have begun without: data already in hand, an event, a new instrument or deployment, a new method or model, a mandate, a surprising observation, a prior result to test, a stated hypothesis, or only a gap in the literature. Each coder also flagged whether its quoted sentence was a gap statement.



Entry state: shares, agreement, what started the work, gap statements, revisits


Figure 7. Entry state under audit.
Figure 7 summarizes the result. Both blind coders kept the problem label for 20 of the 36 problem papers (56%). They moved the rest mostly to capability (5 papers) and to data without theory (3). Labels other than problem were confirmed in 20 of 24 papers. Reweighted to the full round-1 set, the share of problem falls from 78% to about 44% [31, 57]. Each audited paper is weighted by the number of round-1 papers with its batch label divided by the number audited with that label, and the interval comes from a bootstrap that resamples within each label (2,000 resamples). The quote behind a problem label was a gap statement in 84 to 88% of cases, and no other label was ever supported by one. Asked what started the work, the two coders agreed on “a literature gap only” for just 3 of the 36 problem papers and named a concrete object, usually data in hand or a new method, for 22.
Alpha (section 4) for entry state was 0.77 between two runs of the original coder and 0.81 [0.68, 0.92] between the blind coders, but 0.60 to 0.67 between each blind coder and the original, at or below the tentative level of 0.667. The label is consistent within one prompt and moves when the coder is asked what started the work.
We read the entry state as coded so far as a measure of how a paper frames its own beginning, not of how the work began. Neither entry on a problem nor entry on a capability correlates with any outcome (|rho| at most 0.16, q at least 0.19; outcomes.json), so that null result concerns framing. For the next codebook version we propose keeping the framing label and adding a separate operational-start field, whose quote must name the object or act and not a gap.
Limitations of the audit. The blind coders share the batch coder’s model family, so their agreement with each other is not independent evidence, and the 44% depends on their being right. The sample has 60 papers, with only four for each rare label. The audit form asked about the operational start, which may have steered the coders away from problem. A human coding of the same 60 papers is planned but not part of the gold design yet.

title: How Earth-science papers describe their research workflows: the roadmap experiments, round 1
text:
5. What workflows look like



Coded workflows


Figure 8. Node use, steps per paper, entry state and claim status, 233 round-1 papers.
What the labels record. Every label below is read from the published account. Some are framing-level by construction: entry state (section 4.1), claim status and the gates record what the text says. Others are closer to the process the paper reports, such as the nodes used and the V checks, but they too are the paper’s account, not the work (section 10, item 3). Only entry state has had a construct audit. Hypothesize rivals (H) is the next candidate: it appears in 81% of papers, while 3% enter on a hypothesis and 3% pass the action gate, which suggests the coder marks rival explanations named anywhere in the text. A blind audit of H and of decisive mode, on the design of section 4.1, is proposed.
Nodes. Keep (K) appears in all 233 papers, compare (C) in 99%, question (Q) in 98%, vary and replicate (V) in 97%, observe (O) in 92%, infer (I) in 82% and hypothesize rivals (H) in 81%. Explore (E), establishing that a phenomenon is real, appears in only 15%. Protect (P), revising an auxiliary assumption to keep a hypothesis, appears in 34%.
Length and returns. The median paper has 22 coded steps (range 11 to 32; 20 after merging consecutive repeats of a node). Papers return to modes they have already used, a median of 9 times, and 31% report a return after a failed attempt. Revisits, the steps whose node already occurred earlier in the walk (consecutive repeats included), have a median of 12; this is the revisit count used in sections 6 and 7. The merged step count is 18 in the lowest citation quintile and 23 in the highest (21, 20 and 20.5 between).
The textbook order. The rule is the one in g13_calc1_results.py: the merged node sequence must contain question, hypothesize, simulate, design, find conditions, observe, compare (Q, H, S, D, F, O, C) in that order, with any other steps allowed in between. Only 1 of 233 papers does, and none has the seven as a contiguous run. The shorter order question, hypothesize, compare (Q before H before C, gaps allowed) is in 160 papers (69%), and Q, H, D, O, C in 45 (19%). An earlier draft gave 0 of 233; that came from the share stored by g13 rounded to two decimals (1/233 rounds to 0.00), and the count is now stored in report_numbers.json (workflow.textbook_order).
Entry and end. 78% of papers enter on a problem and 11% on a new capability. Anomalies, challenged results, hypotheses, data without theory and external goals share the rest, 2 to 3% each, with the caveat of section 4.1. Outcomes are exclusive, one per paper: 226 papers (97%) keep a claim and 7 (3%) contradict an earlier published claim; none ends with an excluded rival or no conclusion. A paper that contradicts a published claim is coded contradicted, not kept, even though it keeps its own result. Claim status: capability characterized 33%, best explanation 31%, estimate with resolution 21%, regularity in range 12%, confirmed 3% (8 papers). Separately, the claim gate asks only whether the main claim faced a test it could have failed (no rivals required): 17% of papers pass it, and 3% pass the action gate (a stated hypothesis directed the main data acquisition).
Is the entry revisited in the walk? The entry state is one label per paper, so only the entry node can recur. It returns after another node in 33% of the 233 walks (23% of problem papers, 84% of capability papers). No paper reframes its question after a failed attempt: none of the 101 return-after-failure steps sits at Q or is followed by Q (g21_entry_state.py step 4).
Decisive node and composition. The decisive mode is methods in 29% of papers, estimation in 22%, simulation 11%, reconstruction 11%, observation 8%. Half the papers (51%) fit none of the named compositions. Trace series fits 24%, capability first 13% and nature’s repetition 9%; independent replication and strong inference fit fewer than 2% each.
Checks. 97% of papers have full V status: at least one check of the result performed in the paper itself that is more than a rerun (a partial status, reruns only, does not occur; 3% have none). Kinds performed: control 87%, robustness 64%, replication 51%, second method 50%, generalization 22%, reproduction 9%. The control share is high partly because the kind is broad (section 3): synthetic tests, laboratory blanks, reference stations and null models all count. A third (33%) triangulate, with two or more checks of different kinds among replication, method and generalization.



Node transitions


Figure 9. Share of papers with each node-to-node transition, and the 12 most common.
Transitions. 185 of the 210 possible directed transitions occur at least once. The most common are compare to vary (55% of papers), vary to compare (46%), infer to vary (46%), infer to compare (45%) and compare to keep (44%). The workflow is a loop of inference, comparison and checking more than a line from question to answer. Geoscientists will recognize it: invert, compare with data, test against synthetics or a second method, compare again. For NLP readers: as a sequence-labelling output the walks are long (median 22 steps over 15 labels) and dense in transitions (185 of 210 seen), so a model of them needs loops, not a linear template.
