text:
6. Workflows by field and venue



Workflows and outcomes by field and venue


Figure 10. (a) Node use and decisive mode by subfield; (b) workflow length, revisits and citation by journal family; (c) the confounding check of section 7. Subfields are labelled with their dominant topic where one holds at least 60% of coded papers: Artificial Intelligence is 100% seismology, Atmospheric Science 72% cryosphere.
g20_topics_journals.py tests each workflow feature against subfield and against journal family. Binary and categorical features get a permutation chi-square test; counts get a Kruskal-Wallis test (Kruskal & Wallis, 1952). A permutation test builds its null distribution by shuffling the group labels many times (5,000 here) and asks how often a shuffle gives an association as strong as the observed one; it assumes no distribution. Because 104 tests are run, p values are adjusted by the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995): a result with q < 0.1 belongs to a set in which about 10% of findings are expected to be false on average, provided the tests are independent or positively dependent. Effect sizes are bias-corrected Cramér’s V for categorical features and epsilon squared, the share of rank variance explained by the grouping, for counts. Groups with fewer than 10 coded papers are pooled: Geology 9 and Ocean Engineering 4; Elsevier 9, Oxford 6, SSA 2, AAAS 1 and other 1.
28 of 104 tests have q < 0.1, with Cramér’s V from 0.15 to 0.36 (0.19 to 0.36 for single binary features; this V is the effect size, not the node V) and epsilon squared from 0.06 to 0.15.

Field. Seismology (OpenAlex: Artificial Intelligence) papers have methods as the decisive mode in 76% (13 of 17; 51 points above the rest) and use the new-capability node in 88%. The same 17 perform the most kinds of check (median 4, against 2 to 3 elsewhere). Earth-Surface Processes papers (geological formations, aeolian and coastal topics) rely on reconstruction from traces: reconstruction is decisive in 42% (35 points above the rest) and the trace-series composition fits 54% (34 points above). Water Science and Technology papers, mostly watershed hydrology, rarely protect a hypothesis (P in 7%, 28 points below).
Venue. Workflow length differs by family (epsilon squared 0.15): median 24.5 steps for AGU (n = 16), 24 for Copernicus, 19.5 for Wiley non-AGU. Revisits follow (0.11). Copernicus papers use protect in 52%, 24 points above the rest. Springer Nature non-portfolio papers use the simulation mode 33 points less often. All 16 AGU papers use the methods mode. Because families differ in topic as well as in format (section 2), these are family contrasts, not pure venue effects.
No difference. Entry state differs neither by subfield (q 0.95) nor by family (q 0.22).

The 16 AGU papers are not a random draw from AGU. They are the AGU papers whose PDF existed at the first coding. All 16 are open access, against 54 of the 82 eligible AGU papers not coded, and their median cnp is 0.80, against 0.65. Geophysical Research Letters (GRL), a letters journal with a length limit, supplies 2 of the 16 coded papers and 24 of the 82 uncoded ones; the Journal of Geophysical Research sections, full-length journals, supply 9 and 40 (report_numbers.json, calc1.agu_selection). The AGU contrasts in length and in citation may therefore come from selecting open-access, mostly full-length AGU papers. They cannot be read as venue properties until the top-up is coded, and workflow length should then be compared within letters and full-length journals separately.
For NLP readers, the field results are a sanity check: a coder that gives Earth-Surface Processes papers reconstruction and the seismology group methods responds to paper content rather than filling a fixed template. This does not show that the codings are correct. The OpenAlex classifier and the coder respond to the same title, abstract and method vocabulary (13 of the 17 seismology papers have ML terms in their codings), and a model could assign these labels from the abstract alone. An ablation that codes a subset from title and abstract only would show how much of the field pattern needs the full text; only a human comparison can show correctness. For geoscientists, the venue results raise a question this design cannot answer. Longer workflows in AGU and Copernicus papers may reflect what authors do, what those journals let them write, or what the coder can see in longer papers.

title: How Earth-science papers describe their research workflows: the roadmap experiments, round 1
text:
7. Workflows and outcomes
Outcome metrics. All come from OpenAlex through g04_metrics.py, retrieved October 2026, about four years after publication.







Metric
Definition




cnp (impact)
OpenAlex citation normalized percentile: the paper’s citation count as a percentile among works of the same OpenAlex subfield, publication year and type, 0 to 1. The comparison set follows the OpenAlex subfield label, so the 17 seismology papers filed under Artificial Intelligence are ranked against 2022 AI works; their median cnp (0.69) is not comparable with other subfields. Round 1 was drawn with equal numbers per cnp quintile, so the sample is stratified on this outcome (section 2).


fwci (impact)
Field-weighted citation impact: citations divided by the mean citations of comparable works (same subfield, year, type); 1 is the world average. OpenAlex computes it; g04_metrics.py does not record its citation window. Citations are right-skewed, so the median paper sits below 1. The same Artificial Intelligence caveat applies.


novelty_pair (novelty)
Rarity of the paper’s two leading OpenAlex topics appearing together in 2017-2021: −log10(1 + number of 2017-2021 works tagged with both). Higher is rarer. A proxy for an unusual combination, not a measure of novelty.


breadth_refs (breadth)
Share of the paper’s classified references whose primary topic is outside geoscience. Geoscience means OpenAlex fields 19 (Earth and Planetary Sciences) and 23 (Environmental Science), corrected by a hand audit that reassigns geoscience topics filed elsewhere (private/analysis/success-set/breadth/topic_audit.csv).


breadth_citers (breadth)
Share of citing works 2022-2026 outside geoscience, self-citations removed; defined only for papers with at least 10 such citers (53 of 233). Tested in g17; too sparse for the field and venue analyses.


advance
Blind rating of the contribution by the four lab coders of section 4, on the Scientific Advance Profile v1 (ratings v1.0.0). Not yet measured.



cnp and fwci are field-normalized by OpenAlex. novelty_pair and breadth_refs are not, so they differ by subfield from field structure alone. In the coded set the medians are cnp 0.546, fwci 0.482, novelty_pair −3.821 and breadth_refs 0.033. cnp and fwci rank-correlate at 0.99, so they are one impact signal, not two. The other outcomes are nearly independent of each other (|rho| at most 0.12, except the two breadth measures at 0.30).
Because round 1 has equal numbers per cnp quintile, the cnp distribution in the sample is flatter than in the pool. The correlations with cnp below describe this stratified sample and are not estimates for the pool; round 2 is stratified the same way (equal numbers per cnp quintile within each ring, g18_round2_draw.py), so neither round estimates the pool’s cnp distribution; a pool-level estimate would need design weights.



Workflow features against outcomes


Figure 11. Spearman correlations for 245 feature-outcome tests, the 15 with q < 0.1, and correlations among outcomes.
Tests (experiment E6). g17_outcomes.py correlates 49 workflow features (listed in the appendix) with the five outcomes. That gives 245 Spearman rank correlations. Each has a 95% bootstrap interval (2,000 resamples of papers; a bootstrap recomputes the statistic on samples drawn with replacement to see how much it varies), a two-sided permutation p (5,000 shuffles), and a Benjamini-Hochberg q over all 245. Fifteen have q < 0.1, of which about 1.5 are expected to be false on average under the Benjamini-Hochberg assumptions. |rho| ranges from 0.18 to 0.57. Under the stricter Benjamini-Yekutieli correction, which is the Benjamini-Hochberg q multiplied by the sum of 1/i over the 245 tests (6.08) and is valid under any dependence (Benjamini & Yekutieli, 2001), none of the 245 passes; the smallest q is 0.149. The dependence here is strong: cnp and fwci correlate at 0.99, and features such as steps, revisits and distinct nodes overlap. With 5,000 permutations no p can fall below 0.0002, which also bounds the smallest q. No analysis was pre-registered, and the analyst choices below (the pooling cutoff of 10, the stratified estimator, the reference-count adjustment) were made after seeing the data. Round 2 is the confirmatory test, as the PI decided on October 27, 2026. The plan was frozen and published before any round-2 coding existed (preregistration/round2-confirmatory.json, written by g23_confirmatory.py freeze): the 15 associations of this section and the 28 field and venue associations with q < 0.1 in TOPICS.md section 3, 43 tests in one family, each confirmed when its round-2 Benjamini-Hochberg q is below 0.1 and its direction matches round 1, with the same g17 and g20 code. Both rounds are also reported pooled for description, with round as a stratum; that analysis is not part of the test.

Breadth. Methods as decisive mode (0.22), capability first (0.22) and more kinds of V check (0.20) go with broader references. Using the synthesis mode (−0.22), more distinct modes (−0.22) and the infer node (−0.18) go with narrower ones.
Impact. More steps (rho 0.23 with cnp and with fwci), more revisits (0.21, 0.22) and simulation as the decisive mode (0.20, 0.21) go with higher field-normalized citation. Because cnp and fwci are one signal, these are three associations, not six.
Novelty. Papers using the observation mode have rarer topic pairs (0.21).

A check of the coder, not an outcome result. The two largest correlations are between the items borrowed from other fields and breadth_refs (rho 0.57) and between the number of fields borrowed from and breadth_refs (0.51). The coder lists borrowed concepts, methods, instruments or data from the paper’s text; breadth_refs counts references outside geoscience from the OpenAlex reference list. These are two measures of the same thing, one from the text and one from the reference list, so their agreement is a convergent validity check of the coder, not a finding about workflows and outcomes. It holds at 0.52 to 0.57 within every stratification below, and the count repeats well between runs (Spearman 0.87 between the two codings of the retest sample).
Reference count. Longer papers have more references, and papers with more references are cited more. Reference count correlates with cnp at 0.28 and with steps at 0.26. With reference count held fixed by partial correlation (feature and outcome ranks each regressed on the rank of reference count, then the residuals correlated), steps against cnp falls from 0.23 to 0.17, revisits to 0.15, and decisive simulation falls slightly, from 0.20 to 0.19.
Field or venue: the confounding check. g20_topics_journals.py recomputes each of the 15 associations within strata. Ranks are centred inside each subfield, each journal family, or each subfield-by-family cell, so only variation inside a stratum counts, and the permutation shuffles outcomes only within strata. An association survives if it keeps its sign and has q < 0.1 over the 45 stratified tests (Figure 10c). Within subfield, 15 of 15 survive (14 with a bootstrap interval excluding 0). Within journal family, 15 of 15 survive (12 with an interval excluding 0). Within subfield × family, 12 of 15 survive (8).
Stratifying by subfield leaves the associations unchanged; stratifying by family weakens the citation link. The strata are small (8 subfield groups, several with 10 to 17 papers), so this check has little power to detect confounding by subfield. Within subfield, steps against cnp is unchanged (0.225 against 0.227). Within journal family it roughly halves (0.12 [−0.00, 0.25]) yet still survives at q 0.085. A permutation q and a bootstrap interval can disagree near the threshold because they answer different questions: the permutation p asks how often shuffled outcomes give an association this strong, while the interval describes how much the estimate varies when papers are resampled. Within subfield × family, steps against cnp, steps against fwci and revisits against fwci all lose q < 0.1. A likely reason is in section 6: AGU and Copernicus papers have longer workflows and are also more cited. Median cnp is 0.80 for AGU, 0.65 for Copernicus and 0.43 for Wiley non-AGU (epsilon squared 0.13 by family, against 0.08 by subfield). The AGU median rests on the 16 selected papers of section 6. Decisive simulation against citation holds within subfield (0.18 to 0.19), within family (0.17 to 0.18) and within subfield × family (0.13 to 0.14, the fwci interval spanning 0).
Two cautions. First, family is the stratifier most affected by the coverage skew of section 2 (16 AGU and 9 Elsevier papers coded, the AGU papers selected as described in section 6), so this check must be redone after the top-up. Second, the estimator matters: recomputing ranks inside each family, instead of centring pooled ranks, gives 0.165 [0.015, 0.302] rather than 0.120 for steps against cnp (report_numbers.json, confounding.family_estimators). Neither choice makes this a causal statement. Citations at four years measure attention, and a longer workflow may simply be a longer paper.

title: How Earth-science papers describe their research workflows: the roadmap experiments, round 1
section: 8. What peer review changes, and whether papers show it
text:
8. What peer review changes, and whether papers show it



Review visibility


Figure 12. Review changes by how they appear in the paper, absent share by node, and per paper.
Why open review. Most Copernicus journals, including the EGU journals, use interactive public discussion. The submitted manuscript appears online as a discussion paper (a citable preprint), referee comments and author replies are posted beside it, and the final paper is published separately with its review history public. Two Copernicus journals in this sample, European Journal of Mineralogy and Scientific Drilling, published for other societies, do not. For NLP readers, this is a rare case where the revision history of a scientific text is a public record that can be aligned with its final version. In 2022 it covers journals such as The Cryosphere, Hydrology and Earth System Sciences and Geoscientific Model Development.
Data (experiment E3). 64 coded round-1 papers are in Copernicus journals, and 61 have an open discussion; the other three, in European Journal of Mineralogy and Scientific Drilling, have none. g15_open_review.py retrieved 134 referee comments, 147 author comments, community and editor comments, the comment supplements, the review files (author-response PDFs, tracked-changes manuscripts, manuscript versions) and the final article XML for all 61. The coder (claude-opus-5-5, same settings as section 3; the batch took 15.6 hours) read the published PDF, the publisher XML text and discussion.txt, the discussion comments (referee, author, community and editor) with their supplements. The tracked-changes manuscripts, author-response PDFs and manuscript versions were downloaded for all 58 papers but not given to the coder (report_numbers.json, review.coder_input). The coder then wrote a second, review sequence for each paper: one step per change or refusal recorded in the discussion, each with a provenance (review-forced, declined) and a trigger (referee, editor, community commenter, author; the 746 steps have 729 referee, 15 commenter, 2 author and 0 editor triggers). 58 codings validated; three failed (two overlong quotes, one schema error). One journal dominates: 33 of the 58 are in The Cryosphere.
Labelling (experiment E4). Each of the 746 review steps was labelled against the published text by two independent Claude agents, with a third adjudicating disagreements (tools/roadmap/workflows/visibility.js, run in Claude Code, no API cost; the workflow does not set or record the model version). The labelers are the same model family as the coder that wrote the review steps, so blind spots they share would not show in their agreement. The four labels:

as revision: the change is in the paper and the paper ties it to review (“as suggested by a reviewer”, an acknowledgement naming the change); a generic thanks to referees does not count;
as planned: the change is in the paper with no sign it came from review;
absent: the review step describes a change to the work and the paper does not contain it;
no change: a declined request, a reply that only argues, or a promise that is not a change.

Every “as revision” or “as planned” label had to carry a quote from the published text with its locator. g16_visibility.py analyze matched each quote against the text. An “absent” label needs no quote, so the 20 absent steps rest on the labelers’ reading alone; they have not been checked against the referee comments and author replies by a person or by a model from another family.
Results. Of the 746 review steps, 166 record no change and 580 change the work. Of those 580, 560 (96.6%) appear in the paper as if planned, 20 (3.4%; bootstrap over papers 1.7% to 5.6%) are absent, and 0 are marked as a revision. With 0 of 58 papers marking any change, the 95% upper bound on the share of such papers that mark a change is about 5.2% (rule of three, 3/58: with 0 events in n trials, the one-sided 95% upper bound is about 3/n; the exact bound is 5.0%), for Copernicus journals with open discussion. The labelers agreed on 720 of 746 steps (96.5%; Cohen’s kappa 0.91, report_numbers.json, vis.labeler_kappa), and all 560 quotes were found verbatim. Cohen’s kappa (Cohen, 1960) is the agreement of two annotators corrected for the agreement expected by chance from each annotator’s label frequencies, (observed − chance) / (1 − chance); 1 is perfect, 0 is chance. Unlike Krippendorff’s alpha it uses each annotator’s own label frequencies for the chance term. Quote existence shows that each quote is in the text, not that it shows the change its label claims; no entailment check (does the quote support the label?) has been run. 44 of the 560 labeler quotes exceed the 25-word limit the labelers were given (vis.quotes_over_25_words). Changes per paper: median 10, range 4 to 18. 13 papers have at least one absent change.
What the labelers could see. They searched the publisher XML text of the final paper, whose converter keeps body text and captions: only 12 of the 58 texts include an acknowledgements section, and none includes the article supplement. A script check independent of the labelers (g19_report_numbers.py, vis.string_scan) searched pdftotext output of the 58 published PDFs. 53 mention reviewers or referees, every time in a thank-you or in the Copernicus review statement, and none uses a phrase that ties content to review (“as suggested by the reviewer”, “in the revised manuscript” and similar). The zero of “as revision” therefore holds on the full PDF text for the phrases searched. Supplements remain unchecked, so a change moved there would be labelled absent.
Which changes go missing. Vary-and-replicate changes (added controls, replications, sensitivity tests) are the most common kind asked for in review. They are also the kind most often promised in a reply but not found in the paper: 13 of 102 are absent, against 7 of 478 for all other nodes together. With papers as the unit, the absent share of V exceeds that of the other nodes by 0.11 [0.04, 0.20] (permutation within papers, q 0.003 over 14 nodes; exploratory). Refusals still change papers. Of the 220 steps the coder marked as declined, 60 are labelled as planned, usually a caveat or a justifying sentence in the final text.
Comparison with the pilot. A nine-paper pilot (October 21) coded loops from Nature peer-review files, EGU discussions and one preprint revision. Of 126 loops, 4 were readable as loops in the paper, 70 were in the paper as if planned and 52 were absent. The direction agrees. The absent share differs (41% against 3.4%), and the reason is not established. One candidate is construction: the pilot counted analyses discussed in review files that never entered any version of the manuscript, while the E3 coder saw the authors’ promises in the discussion with the final paper in view. Reading the final paper may bias the coder toward review steps that the paper contains, and so toward “as planned”. An earlier draft said the EGU sequences were coded from tracked-changes manuscripts; the coder was not given them.
Reading. Not attributing changes to review is the norm in these journals, and their review history is public. A reader, model or agent design that uses only the final articles sees no review loop, and the work most affected is checking. The full account, with methods and references, is in private/text/report-review-visibility.md.

title: How Earth-science papers describe their research workflows: the roadmap experiments, round 1
text:
9. Papers against agent loops



Papers against agent loops


Figure 13. Node use by papers and by agent systems, distinct nodes per workflow, and researcher transitions that agents run.
Agent side. 31 published agent designs were coded blind by two model coders under loop codebook 0.1.2 (private/analysis/reliability/frozen/loop-CODEBOOK-0.1.2.md), which uses the same graph and the same NASEM rule for V. The coders are Claude Code subagents run with the same brief: opus-b uses claude-opus-5-5 and sonnet-c uses claude-sonnet-5-5 (private/analysis/reliability/RUN.md). They range from 17 general patterns and tools, such as ReAct (Yao, Zhao et al., 2023), Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023), tree of thoughts (Yao, Yu et al., 2023) and coding agents, to 14 research systems, such as The AI Scientist (Lu et al., 2026), Coscientist (Boiko et al., 2023), the AI co-scientist (Gottweis et al., 2026), FunSearch (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024) and AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025), Robin (Ghareeb et al., 2026) and Kosmos (Mitchener et al., 2025); the list is agents_manifest.json. A node counts for an agent when the coder marks it full: the loop itself performs the node as the paper codebook defines it, without a person stepping in, from receiving its task until it stops. Shares are averaged over the two coders. The two coders agree on the mark (full, partial or none) in 85% of the 31 × 15 system-node cells, with Krippendorff’s alpha 0.73 over all marks. For geoscientists: an agent loop is the cycle an AI system repeats (propose, act, observe the result, revise). The question is which research moves that cycle contains. For NLP readers, the nodes map onto agent components: Q is task or question proposal, H the generation of competing hypotheses, C evaluation against an external signal, V ablation, seed variation or held-out testing.
The two sides are measured differently. Papers are coded from their full published text under codebook 1.5.0; agents from published design descriptions under the loop codebook. By design an agent usually receives its question from the user, which by itself explains much of the low share at Q. General patterns were never built to do research, so including them lowers agent shares by construction. No check of measurement invariance has been run, such as coding a few agent-system papers’ own reported experiments under codebook 1.5.0.
Results (experiment E5, g14_papers_vs_agents.py). Papers use a median of 10 distinct nodes [10, 11]; agent systems use 3.5 [2, 4.5]. The largest gaps are at question (98% of papers against 10% of agent systems), vary or replicate (97% against 10%), infer (82% against 5%) and hypothesize rivals (81% against 6%). For the 14 research systems alone the shares are higher but the gaps remain: Q 18%, V 21%, I 11%, H 14%; for the 17 general patterns and tools they are 3%, 0%, 0% and 0% (report_numbers.json, agents.node_share_by_group). No agent system protects a hypothesis (P 0%, against 34% of papers) and none triangulates (0% against 33%). Only refine (R) is run more often by agents (68% against 56%), with overlapping intervals. Of the 59 researcher transitions found in at least 10% of papers, 33 (opus-b) or 24 (sonnet-c) are run by any agent. The most common transitions that no agent runs are vary to compare (46% of papers), infer to vary (46%) and vary to infer (37%).
Reading with section 8. Vary and replicate is among the moves agents run least, and it is the work most often added in review and then presented as planned. An agent designed from methods sections would see these checks but not that review forced them.

title: How Earth-science papers describe their research workflows: the roadmap experiments, round 1
text:
10. Limitations

One model family, no human check. Every role is played by a Claude model (table below). Test-retest (section 4) measures agreement of the model with itself, so systematic misreadings that repeat across runs would not show; the entry-state audit points to one candidate. Agreement among coders of the same family is not independent evidence for the screening, the E4 labels, the E5 agent coding or the 4.1 audit. In E4, Claude labels review steps that Claude wrote. Where cost is zero (the Claude Code workflows), a labeler from another model family on a subset of E4 and of the 4.1 audit would be the cheapest independent check.
Sample set by full-text access and download timing. Coded papers are 83% open access, against 46% of uncoded eligible papers, and the venue mix is skewed (section 2). Results on AGU and Elsevier rest on 16 and 9 papers until the top-up returns, and the 16 AGU papers are selected (section 6).
What a paper says is not what was done. The coding records the published account. Section 8 shows one way that account departs from the process.
Machine labels for field and rule-based families. Subfield is OpenAlex’s classifier output for the leading topic, and two subfield names mislead (section 2). Two families rest on DOI prefixes and fall back to “other”: Russian Geology and Geophysics (prefix 10.2113, GeoScienceWorld, which OpenAlex lists under Elsevier; its papers were skipped by the convenor’s decision of October 27) and Seismica. One Remote Sensing of Environment record carries the DOI of its ESS Open Archive preprint (prefix 10.1002, a Wiley prefix), so it counts as Wiley non-AGU. The effect is a few papers per family.
Outcome metrics. Citations are counted at about four years. novelty_pair is a proxy based on topic-pair rarity. breadth_refs and the borrowed-from-other-fields counts measure the same thing (section 7). Advance is not measured.
Many tests. There are 245 outcome tests, 104 workflow tests, 16 coverage tests, 16 outcome-by-group tests and 45 stratified tests, each corrected within its own question. None was pre-registered; all are exploratory and descriptive, and none is causal. Under the Benjamini-Yekutieli correction none of the 245 outcome tests passes.
Small cells. Many subfield × family strata hold one or two papers and drop out. Oceanography (10), the Nature portfolio (14) and Water Science and Technology (14) sit just above the pooling cutoff of 10.
One journal dominates the review study. 33 of the 58 review papers are in The Cryosphere, and all have open discussion. Journals with closed review may differ in either direction.
Round 2 not yet coded. Every workflow and outcome result is round 1 only. Round 2 was designed to test whether those results hold over 157 journals.
Training-data contamination. The papers are from 2022, and the Copernicus discussions, referee comments and replies have been public since then, so they are likely in the coder’s training data. The model may recall published framings or review histories instead of reading the attached text, which bears on the “as planned” labels and on the coding generally. A cheap probe, not run because it costs API money: give the model title and DOI only, ask for entry state, decisive mode and the main review requests, and report how much of the full-text coding it reproduces; or code a few papers published after the model’s training cutoff and compare distributions.
Papers and agents are measured differently. Papers are coded from full text, agents from design descriptions, under different codebooks, and the agent set mixes general patterns with research systems (section 9). Node shares for agents are not directly comparable to shares for papers.

11. Reproducibility
Repositories and commits. The public repository metascience-and-AI is on branch framework-v0.5, latest commit 2798f89. g20_topics_journals.py, g21_entry_state.py, figures/fig11_topics_journals.py, fig12_field_workflows.py and fig13_entry_state.py are not yet committed, and the other figure scripts, g16_visibility.py and g19_report_numbers.py have uncommitted edits. All thirteen figure sidecars, report_numbers.json, topics/topics_journals.json, review/visibility_results.json and entry/entry_state.json therefore carry 2798f89+uncommitted (and, for the figures, ea0f2f9+uncommitted); a commit of both repositories followed by the rebuild below clears the marker. outcomes/outcomes.json, calc1/results.json and calc1/papers_vs_agents.json were written at clean commit 3ec8a49. The private repository private/ is local only, latest commit ea0f2f9. Every output JSON has a _provenance block with script, commit, date, inputs and parameters. Every figure has a sidecar JSON with both commits, the sha256 of every input and every plotted number.
Registry. private/data/roadmap/EXPERIMENTS.md lists each experiment (E0 to E7) with its question, inputs, model, codebook, script, commit, exact command, outputs and cost. Every script appends a line to private/data/roadmap/MANIFEST.md, and selection rules go to DECISIONS.md.
Scripts. Corpus: tools/roadmap/g01 to g12, and g18. Coding: tools/code_papers.py, which spends money and was not rerun for this report. Analysis: g13_calc1_results.py (workflows, test-retest), g14_papers_vs_agents.py, g15_open_review.py, g16_visibility.py, g17_outcomes.py, g19_report_numbers.py (every number no other script writes, including since this draft the between-paper baseline, quote existence, the textbook order, the AGU selection, the within-family estimators, the labelers’ kappa, resubmissions, the retest-sample mix and agent shares by system group; rerun on October 27 for this draft, with no earlier value changed), g20_topics_journals.py and g21_entry_state.py. Validation: tools/check_coding.py.
Rebuild, after committing. The analysis steps spend no money.

Rerunning with an open model. tools/code_papers_open.py export writes the exact system prompt, the per-paper user text, an OpenAI-style requests.jsonl, and an inputs.json with the sha256 of every input text. run sends the same requests to an OpenAI-compatible endpoint (for example OLMo served by vLLM) and validates the results with the same checker. To compare with Claude, run python tools/check_coding.py agree <claude coding> <open-model coding> per paper, or rerun the E2 procedure of g13_calc1_results.py with the open-model folder in place of gold-r2. The step-by-step guide is agents/coder/HANDOFF.md. The pipeline was tested end to end against a mock endpoint on October 27; it has not yet run on a real open model. Its requests set temperature 0, while the Claude codings used the API default, so a Claude against open-model comparison mixes model and decoding differences unless the open model is also run at its default temperature.

section: Appendix: the 49 workflow features of section 7
text:
Appendix: the 49 workflow features of section 7
From g17_outcomes.py, computed on the final-paper sequence; binary features are kept when 10 to n − 10 papers have them.

Counts (9): steps (as coded); distinct nodes; distinct modes; revisits (steps whose node occurred earlier); returns after failure; items borrowed from other fields (imports); fields borrowed from (import fields); novelty claims (statements of novelty the coder lists); kinds of V check performed.
Gates and checks (4): claim gate yes; action gate yes or partly; any return after failure; triangulation. Outcome contradicted (7 papers) and full V status (225 papers) fall outside the 10 to n − 10 filter.
Entry (2): entry on a problem; entry on a capability.
Nodes used (11): D, E, F, H, I, N, O, P, R, S, X (K, C, Q and V are in nearly every paper and drop out).
Modes used (12): estimation, exploration, hypothesis, instruments, methods, observation, reconstruction, regularities, robustness, simulation, synthesis, theory.
Decisive mode (7): estimation, hypothesis, methods, observation, reconstruction, regularities, simulation.
Composition (4): capability first, nature’s repetition, none fits, trace series.

Inquiry-mode ledger

title: Scientific advance: records and evaluation
text:
One row per episode, signed and dated; five minutes at the end of a meeting. Live table.
The central question is what changed scientifically and what justified the next action.
Multiple modes and unknown chronology are allowed. An imagined alternative policy is a counterfactual judgment, not an observed treatment effect.








Field
Record




Episode/source
Identifier, source location, record type, contributor/date.


Question before → after
Include unchanged/unknown. Origin and reframing are different variables.


Action → result
What was done; artifact or observation; what changed.


Modes
IDs and versions, multiple if appropriate; unknown/outside vocabulary permitted.


Gain and warrant
Before/after scientific gain; evidence and supported scope; what remains provisional.


Next action/agent lesson
One useful action, alternative, or testable capability.




Expanded process record: information available at the time, alternatives, assumptions, constraints, discarded paths, commitment history, disciplinary resources, and missing steps.
Keep raw artifacts, contemporaneous statements, and retrospective interpretations distinct (Holmes 1987). Never infer complete chronology from a paper’s rhetorical order.

title: Scientific advance: records and evaluation
text:
Claim record

For substantive findings, conjectures, or capability claims; ordinary tool calls need an action log, not a full novelty search.
One template is shared by the notebook, agent output, and assessment. Preserve the original record and append dated revisions.








Field
Required content




Identity
Claim ID, case/project, date, text, scope; mode IDs and source versions.


Scientific gain
Before/after change and the case-level gain it supports; why that change matters.


Novelty
Reference date, search limits, closest precedent, new component, uncertainty.


Warrant/adequacy
Evidence required/supplied, assumptions, checks and results, unresolved or contradicted components.


Status
Conjectural, provisional, supported within scope, contradicted, or unresolved; assessor/date/reason.


Impact
Observed use with sources/dates; separately, any prediction with target, horizon, and later check.


Dependencies
Data/code/source artifacts and other claims on which this one depends.


Follow-up
Corroborated, challenged, narrowed, overturned, or no informative follow-up located; search date and evidence.




Correct procedure and warranted assertion at a date do not guarantee eventual truth. Continued citation and absence of contradiction do not establish correctness.
Count case-level gains, not claim cards: several claims may support one advance.
Machine-readable template; blank values are prompts for completion, not observed results.

title: Scientific advance: records and evaluation
text:
Novelty Dossier v1

Evaluate an exact contribution against work available at a stated date (Uzzi et al. 2013; Fontana et al. 2020).








Field
Record




Atomic claim
Observation, method, concept, explanation, connection, or question.


Reference frame
Community, corpus, languages, publication cutoff, search date.


Closest precedent
Specific work and overlapping passage/result.


New component
What apparently goes beyond the precedent and in which respect.


Search for equivalents
Earlier terminology, adjacent fields, and searches likely to uncover a precedent.


Limits/judgment
Missing sources; exact/close/component precedent, apparently new component, or unresolved.




“No precedent located within this search” is a bounded finding. A historical replay is not contemporary novelty.
Human judgments are comparators with disagreement (Boudreau et al. 2016). Citation/semantic novelty does not establish correctness or significance.
Candidate checks: paraphrase of a known result; established method with new data; concealed precedent. Report false and missed novelty, and search coverage.

title: Scientific advance: records and evaluation
text:
Scientific Advance Profile v1

Working definition: a meaningful warranted improvement in knowledge, understanding, or research capability. Compare knowledge and understanding accounts (Bird 2007; Dellsén 2016).
State the frame: supplied task/project, historical state of a field, or contemporary knowledge.








Field
Question




Starting state
What was already known, possible, and available to the investigator?


Gain
What can now be known, explained, measured, predicted, or investigated?


Magnitude/significance
Quantitative change where meaningful; why it matters for this scientific question.


Evidence
What warrants the gain, at what uncertainty and scope? What would change the assessment?


Contribution role
Corrective, enabling, integrative, cumulative, transformative; overlap is possible.


Dependencies
Instruments, datasets, methods, people, standards, and prior results.


Consequences
Actual downstream use and time window; distinguish prospective promise.




Primary case outcome: achieved/not demonstrated/unassessable meaningful warranted gain, judged against criteria fixed before evaluation. Unassessable and incomplete cases do not count as successes and stay visible in the full denominator.
Report success fraction by case family/mode, magnitude in scientific units, uncertainty, and all failures. An aggregate is conditional on case selection, not a universal measure of science.
Prespecify meaningful gains and a procedure for assessing unanticipated valid gains; judges must provide evidence and reasons for any such award.
Novelty, warrant, impact, and cost remain visible beside the primary outcome. Avoid a default weighted sum or product.
First assess evidence/gain with venue, citations, and agent identity hidden where feasible. Then reveal documented uptake to assess realized impact. Retain disagreements; calibrate on development cases before freezing the rubric.
Do not rank enabling between incremental and field-shaping: those describe role and reach. A correction or replication can produce a major gain.

title: Scientific advance: records and evaluation
text:
Interdisciplinary transfer profile

Hypothesis: appropriate integration can improve scientific gains; fluent borrowing is insufficient (Wagner et al. 2011; Shi and Evans 2023).
Record source/target concepts, variables, units, scales, assumptions, mathematical or mechanistic correspondence, adaptation, failure conditions, and a check on the target.
Record competence as held, borrowed from an expert, checked through tools/evidence, or missing. Assess depth through demonstrated understanding, not reference concentration.
Compare access to the same cross-field material with/without an explicit transfer procedure. Include beneficial, irrelevant, and invalid transfers.
Assess project gains, individual/team competence, and portfolio diversity separately; effects in one do not establish the others (Kitcher 1990; Leahey et al. 2017; Hao et al. 2026).

title: Scientific advance: records and evaluation
text:
Agent evaluation protocol v1

Follow the historical evaluation specification. Past papers supply scientific reference work, not a compulsory sequence of actions.
Three policies: competent generic planner with the same guidance; hypothesis-testing planner allowed inspection/calibration; planner selecting human-defined modes. A rigid action-gate rule is an optional ablation.
Hold model/version, tools, evidence, budgets, and human assistance comparable; separate mode competence with a supplied mode from mode selection.
Freeze task packets, scoring, information access, costs, stopping rules, and policy versions before evaluation. Record commitments relative to access, not only collection dates (Nosek et al. 2018).
Reserve entire projects/case families to avoid leakage between related development and evaluation episodes. Repeat runs, but do not count repeats as independent scientific cases.
Assess artifacts and actions, not generated accounts of hidden reasoning. Human assessors should be blind to policy where feasible.








Control
What it reveals




Positive and negative cases
Failure to recover a real gain or invention of a gain unsupported by the evidence.


Measurement artifact
Mistaking response/processing for a physical effect.


Missing evidence
Appropriate limitation or next measurement, versus unjustified certainty or generic abstention.


Independent period/region
Transfer beyond the evidence used to formulate the claim.


Valuable correction
Whether a novelty-focused agent misses a consequential correction.


Same guidance without mode structure
Whether improvement comes from mode organization rather than more instructions.




Choose independent cases and outcome thresholds first; use development variability/cost to set repeated-run budgets. No fixed run count guarantees broad evidence.
The initial reference sample permits bounded comparisons. A population claim needs the corpus study.

title: Is there a scientific method?
text:
Central question
Meeting 1 of 13
Discussed v0.4 · held September 15, 2026 · record discussion
Is hypothesis-testing a universal account of inquiry, a standard for justification, or one useful mode among several?
crumbs: 1  Is there a scientific method?

title: Is there a scientific method?
text:
Anchor and companion

Everyone reads the selected anchor sections and the companion abstract/overview. The rotating reader presents the companion in depth.
Pairing: Methodological ideal / evidential counterpoint. Full records and access notes: bibliography.


Anchor
Platt, J. R. (1964). Strong Inference. Science, 146(3642), 347–353. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.146.3642.347
Read Platt in full. Identify the role of alternative explanations and discriminating observations.


Companion
Cleland, C. E. (2001). Historical science, experimental science, and the scientific method. Geology, 29(11), 987–990. https://doi.org/10.1130/0091-7613(2001)029%3C0987:HSESAT%3E2.0.CO;2
Read Cleland’s Geology paper in full. It makes the argument in four pages, for geologists.
crumbs: 1  Is there a scientific method?

title: Is there a scientific method?
text:
Why these readings belong together
Platt offers a prescriptive strategy; Cleland analyzes differences between experimental interventions and reconstructing past events. Neither paper directly records this group’s daily research. Test both against an actual project rather than declaring one a complete scientific method. (Platt 1964; Cleland 2001)
crumbs: 1  Is there a scientific method?

title: Is there a scientific method?
section: Where the two papers sit on the unit graph
text:
Where the two papers sit on the unit graph

Read the unit of inquiry first. It defines deduction, induction, abduction, hypothesis, and the verbs test, confirm, exclude, and corroborate, and draws one unit of hypothesis testing as a workflow of nine nodes, Q to R.
Both papers are overlays on that graph. Neither adds a node.


Platt

Strong inference is the parallel composition of unit page, section 6: \(n\) units with their own S share one D, F, O, and C; the figure below draws it with the unit’s letters (Platt 1964, 347).
What makes it strong is one property of node D: every outcome at C excludes at least one rival. The tree branches and prunes on each pass.
Platt’s step 3, “carrying out the experiment so as to get a clean result” (Platt 1964, 347), is where node V hides. He never describes the control series; Cleland says it is most of the work (Cleland 2002, 477–78).
Its parts are older than Platt: Bacon’s eliminative induction at D and X, Chamberlin’s family at H, Popper’s asymmetry at X (Platt 1964, 349–50).
Platt supplies nothing at H beyond “invent” and sends the reader to Pólya (Platt 1964, 347). The generative step is outside the method.
Fifty years on: whether strong inference described practice or inspired it (Davis 2006), and how it is cited now (Fudge 2014).
Platt says the scheme is Baconian: the conditional inductive tree, the instances of the fingerpost, induction by rejections and exclusions (Platt 1964, 349–50; Bacon 2004); Chamberlin’s multiple working hypotheses round it out (Platt 1964, 350; Chamberlin 1965); Popper supplies the asymmetry at X (Platt 1964, 350).
The exclusion step contradicts \(H_i + A\), not \(H_i\) alone. Platt does not draw the distinction; Cleland makes it the centre of her case, with Neptune as the example (Cleland 2001, 988).

Figure 1.1: Platt’s strong inference as a composition of units: three units share one crucial experiment. Each rival gets its own derivation at S; one design D picks the observable on which the three expectations differ; a single F, O, and C serve all three; each outcome excludes two rivals and keeps one; the survivor is refined at R and the cycle returns to H. Node V is drawn dashed because Platt’s step 3, ‘a clean result’, stands where the control series would be and he does not describe it. Letters are those of graph v0.4.2.







Cleland

Her thesis in one sentence: two patterns of evidential reasoning, “from causes (test conditions) to effects, with the concomitant worries about ruling out false positives and false negatives, and from effects (traces) to causes, with the concomitant worries about ruling out alternative explanations” (Cleland 2002, 484–85). The first runs S, D, F, O, C, V; the second runs O, H, K.









Node
Objection
Where she says it




F
Controlled experiments are impossible for past events: the time frame is too long, the conditions too complex. A smoking gun already exists; it is uncovered by fieldwork, not produced by varying conditions
Cleland (2001), p. 988; Cleland (2002), p. 484


V
Little in historical research resembles controlling for false positives and negatives. Generating rivals is not entertaining auxiliaries: an auxiliary is independent of \(H\) and can be dropped to save it; rivals are incompatible with \(H\)
Cleland (2002), pp. 483–484


X
Refutation hits the conjunction; in practice \(A\) is revised first. Astronomers kept Newton and found Neptune
Cleland (2001), p. 988


K
The smoking gun is a retention move, inference to the best explanation within a stated set of rivals; it can be deposed later, and it need not touch the rivals: shocked quartz is “merely irrelevant” to the contagion hypothesis
Cleland (2002), pp. 481–483


before H
An exploratory phase in which the phenomenon is not yet stable and no \(H\) is worth deriving from; explore until it repeats, then test. Becquerel, Faraday, Cech; Viking as the case where the controls were fixed before any data
Cleland (2002), pp. 479–480, 486




Her positive claim, the asymmetry of overdetermination, is why the found-\(C\) path works: a past event leaves many independent traces, so O can be repeated on new traces without control (Cleland 2001, 989–90; 2002, 487–90). Both papers allow that it may be probabilistic rather than strict (Cleland 2001, 989; 2002, 490–91).
The two patterns are not tied to fields. Experimentalists reason like historians when a test fails or a phenomenon surprises them; historians reason like experimentalists when nature repeats herself, as with Cepheid variables, though without the power to set or remove the test condition (Cleland 2002, 485–86). That last case is the statistical mode of this seminar: an earthquake catalog is nature’s repeated experiment.
A smoking gun can be predicted before it is found (Dicke’s background radiation) or stumbled on (the Alvarez iridium) (Cleland 2001, 990). Prediction versus accommodation cuts across the historical and experimental divide.
Cleland’s answer to why the earth sciences do not recognize themselves in the textbook: their hypotheses are about particular past events, not regularities (Cleland 2002, 480); the evidence is traces that already exist; and the taught account and the practiced one differ. Three geologists’ textbook says “hypotheses cannot be proved, only disproved,” while the field’s practice is a hunt for positive evidence (Cleland 2001, 988; 2002, 483). Philosophers made it worse by describing historical science as narrative, which fits archaeology and not geology or astronomy (Cleland 2002, 475). Computer simulation does not change the historical character of the hypotheses (Cleland 2001, 987, 989).



Read against the texts, September 16, 2026

Basis: all three papers read in full. Cleland 2002 from the publisher’s PDF at Cambridge Core; Platt and Cleland 2001 from copies posted on university course pages, not stored in this repository. Page numbers are the journals’ own. What follows is what the notes above and the sealed analysis had not recorded.

In Platt, and not in the notes

The yardstick (p. 351): surveys, taxonomy, instrument design, systematic measurement, and theoretical computation “have their proper and honored place, provided they are parts of a chain of precise induction.” Platt subordinates every other mode to the loop. The assigned paper is the textual opponent of the glossary’s pluralism.
The two boxes (pp. 351–352): “The logical box is coarse but strong. The mathematical box is fine-grained but flimsy.” Five-decimal agreement excludes; one- or two-decimal fit “may be a trap”; “we substitute correlations for causal studies.” Bohr and Schrödinger predict the same Rydberg constant, so agreement alone excludes nothing. Platt’s position on the statistical and estimation modes, and on data-driven discovery, is here, and it is the equifinality problem of meeting 9.
Pasteur (p. 351): moving to a new biological problem every two or three years and beating experts who “knew a hundred times as much,” which Platt attributes to method, not knowledge. The assigned paper’s own breadth claim, for meeting 11.
When the method pays (p. 349): in “high-information” fields, where the hypothesis space is large or observations are expensive, and where leadership taught it. Platt’s own contingency claim about method and field speed, testable in the corpus study.
The loop in hardware (p. 349): coincidence circuits that “run through a complete logical tree in a microsecond.” The first automated excluder in the paper.
The pathologies (p. 350): the Frozen Method, the Eternal Surveyor, the Never Finished, the Great Man With a Single Hypothesis, the Little Club of Dependents, the Vendetta, the All-Encompassing Theory. The glossary uses one of the seven; the list is a ready-made failure taxonomy.
Platt’s evidence: the published form of papers (Lederberg’s “subject to denial” list, Monod and Jacob’s “logical density,” a 1964 paper’s “our conclusions might be invalid if”), notebooks (Faraday, Fermi), and recollected meetings (Szilard at Boulder, 1958), pp. 348, 351–352. Method read off narratives: standing question 5 applied to the paper itself.
Footnote 14: Platt cites Kuhn 1962 and says the modified view “does not invalidate any of these conclusions.” He knew the objection.

In Cleland 2001, and not in the notes

The schema is hers (p. 987): a test implication, if \(C\) then \(E\), inferred from \(H\); auxiliaries on p. 988. The unit page’s formula comes from the assigned reading.
Two textbook accounts, inductivism and falsificationism, both “deeply flawed, both logically and as accounts of the actual practices of scientists” (pp. 987–988). The paper answers the question of what the original thinkers proposed, in one page.
Experimentalists control, they do not falsify (pp. 988, 990): after a failure they vary auxiliaries against false negatives; after a success they vary them again, and remove \(C\), against false positives. “They are not trying to disprove their hypotheses or to save them from falsification.”
A smoking gun can be predicted (Dicke) or stumbled on (Alvarez), p. 990.
Laboratory work in historical science sharpens traces or tests an auxiliary (Miller-Urey), p. 989. Computer models determine consequences under stated conditions and cannot say which conditions obtained: snowball Earth, p. 989. Meeting 9.
The probabilistic loosening of overdetermination is already in the short paper (p. 989), not only in the long one.

In Cleland 2002, and not in the notes

The unit is the series, not the test (pp. 477–478): “The historical tendency of philosophers to take the isolated experiment as the descriptive unit of experimental research has obscured this character.” Each experiment is designed in light of the last; without such a series “most researchers are reluctant to submit their work.” This is the finding that added node V to the unit graph.
Rivals are not auxiliaries (pp. 483–484): an auxiliary is independent of \(H\) and can be dropped to save it; rivals are incompatible with \(H\). This is why H and P are different nodes.
The one-sentence thesis (pp. 484–485): causes to effects with false-positive and false-negative worries; effects to causes with rival-explanation worries.
Nature repeats herself (p. 485): Cepheid variables give a body of evidence “resembling what an experimental program would provide,” without the power to set or remove the test condition. The statistical mode, in the assigned philosophy.
Experimental hypotheses “postulate regularities among event-types,” which “may be statistical” and “may or may not be causal” (p. 476, note 2). Cleland places functional regularities inside experimental science’s own objects.
Two criteria for a good historical explanation, unification (Kitcher) and a causal mechanism (Salmon); acceptance of drift waited for the mechanism (p. 481). Meeting 4.
Independent smoking guns (p. 491): microspherules, fullerenes, soot; “had iridium been absent” the case would stand. Convergence of independent traces, which is the evidence column of the synthesis mode.
Lakatos: a “superficial resemblance”; he ignored protection against misleading confirmations (p. 478 and note 4).
Her idealization (p. 476): “simple, idealized experiments,” setting aside Franklin’s complications with instruments and unrepeatable experiments. The limit of her account for meeting 5.

Corrections made to these pages from the reading

The Bacon citation moved from p. 349 to pp. 349–350; “proper rejections and exclusions” is on 350.
The “conditions found, not set” objection now cites Cleland 2002, p. 484, where she says it, with 2001, p. 988, for the impossibility of controlled experiments.
The unit graph gained node V, the control series, and the verb table gained “control.”



What to settle in the room

Are Platt’s exclusion at X and Cleland’s smoking gun at K one Bayesian move under two constraints, or two different moves? Cleland’s last sentence says one (Cleland 2002, 495); the two papers read as two.
Both papers put the hard part before the loop: Platt at H, Cleland in the exploratory phase before it.
crumbs: 1  Is there a scientific method?

title: Is there a scientific method?
text:
Held September 15, 2026

Source: the group’s shared meeting notes for September 15. No slides are recorded for this meeting. Beyond the anchor and companion, the discussion drew on two readings listed elsewhere on this site: the science-of-science review Fortunato et al. (2018) and Simon’s argument that discovery has a logic, Simon (1973), an optional reading for meeting 13. The group has since identified Klahr and Simon’s review, Klahr and Simon (1999), as the source of the discussion of prior knowledge; it was read in full on September 23, 2026, from a copy supplied by the convenor and not stored here. Simon (1973) has not been read for this page.


What was discussed



Reading
Role on this page
What the room took from it




Platt (1964)
Anchor
Strong inference (the notes say “strong hypothesis”); falsification between rivals as the method


Cleland (2001)
Companion
Assume the conditions, derive the predicted event, test the hypothesis by whether it occurs; the smoking gun as the evidence that discriminates between hypotheses


Fortunato et al. (2018)
Background, cited in the glossary
Science grows and changes, so a data-driven science of science can show where opportunities for advance remain; small teams against large teams; how scientists choose experiments


Simon (1973)
Optional reading, meeting 13; not read for this page
Where new ideas come from; discovery as search; the British Museum algorithm against heuristic search


Klahr and Simon (1999)
Identified after the meeting; read in full
Starting knowledge and the path of search; discovery as problem solving in several spaces





What the room said

The scientific method, as the room stated it. A hypothesis \(H\) is stated, conditions \(C\) are assumed, and a testable implication is derived: if \(C\) is brought about, event \(E\) will occur. \(H\) is accepted or rejected according to whether \(E\) occurs.
Three kinds of cognitive work, induction, deduction, and abduction, and a fourth element, the conditions, which are “never really fully represented and reproducible.”
Prior knowledge sets the range of hypotheses. With strong prior knowledge the range is narrow and the work is a hunt for the smoking gun that shows the expectation is right; with little prior knowledge the range is broader.
Two textbook accounts. Inductivism: repeated successes confirm H. Falsificationism: H cannot be confirmed, only refuted.
Less difference between experimental and historical science than Cleland draws.
The smoking gun cuts both ways. It discriminates between hypotheses, and it biases the work toward confirming one.
Falsification is not done as rigorously as Chamberlin and Platt describe, because conditions vary. Falsifying a hypothesis needs conditions that are known, met, and repeated, which is very hard in nature; a failed prediction can be a misleading disconfirmation.
Models of the past are theory. The notes quote Cleland: “modeling past events is theoretical work, and while it may yield predictions, these predictions are only as secure as the assumptions upon which the model is based.”
Science of science. Small teams bring in older, less popular ideas and open new directions, and last longest when they keep a stable core; large teams refine recent, popular ideas and reach high but often short-lived impact. Scientists’ actual strategy for choosing experiments mines the hubs they already care about efficiently but does not reveal the whole knowledge network; both high-impact targets and unexplored ones need attention. There are optimal team sizes, and smaller teams try to disrupt. The design question the room drew: how to build a small, stable core of agents.
Simon: discovery is search. If some ways of hunting for hypotheses are systematically better than others, discovery has a logic. It does not need to solve the problem of induction: discovery recodes the data in hand into a more compact pattern, and whether the pattern fits those data can be checked with certainty; whether it will hold on future data belongs to testing. Brute-force enumeration, the British Museum algorithm, against heuristic search, which uses structure in the data to prune the space. Generating hypotheses is a search process, some search processes are demonstrably better than others, and studying why gives a logic of discovery.
What the group needs to quantify next: disruptive ideas, scientific consensus, novelty, and what counts as an advance, a big leap against incremental work. Meeting 10 took up novelty and uptake the following week, on September 22.



Read against the texts

The room’s definition is Cleland’s schema without the auxiliaries. Cleland writes the test implication as “if \(C\) then \(E\),” inferred from \(H\) (Cleland 2001, 987), and adds the auxiliary assumptions a page later (Cleland 2001, 988). The room’s remark that conditions are never fully represented is the same point from the other side: what is not written into \(C\) sits in \(A\), and a failed prediction cannot say which conjunct failed (Duhem 1954). The unit graph writes the schema as \(H + A + C \Rightarrow E\) for that reason.
On falsification, the room agrees with Cleland against Platt. Cleland’s own claim is that experimentalists “are not trying to disprove their hypotheses”: after a failed prediction they vary the auxiliaries to guard against a false negative, the room’s misleading disconfirmation (Cleland 2001, 988). What the room calls unrigorous falsification is, in her account, the control series, node V on the graph (Cleland 2002, 477–78). Where conditions can only be found, V is unavailable, and the found-C methods replace it with independent traces.
“Less difference than Cleland draws” is partly hers. She allows that experimentalists reason like historians when a test fails or a result surprises them, and that historians reason like experimentalists when nature repeats herself (Cleland 2002, 485–86). What she maintains is the asymmetry of overdetermination: a past event leaves many independent traces (Cleland 2001, 989–90). The notes do not record the room disputing that. Whether the difference is one of kind or of degree stays open.
The smoking gun and confirmation bias. Cleland’s defense is that a smoking gun is judged within a stated set of rivals, and the survivor is retained as the best explanation, not proved (Cleland 2002, 481–82). The bias the room named is the risk when the set is too small, which is Chamberlin’s warning against the ruling theory (Chamberlin 1965). On the graph, that is why H requires at least two incompatible rivals and why K records “best explanation within the stated set.”
Prior knowledge narrows H in both directions. It supplies hypotheses by analogy (Gilbert 1886), and it hides the rivals nobody thought to list. The notes’ contrast, narrow range with prior knowledge, broad range without, is a claim about the size of the rival set at H that the ledger can record case by case.
Klahr and Simon on starting knowledge. The review does not say that prior knowledge predetermines the path. It documents two narrowing effects: familiarity with a domain biases which hypotheses seem plausible, and plausible ones are tested first (Klahr and Simon 1999, 538); and recognition can transfer negatively, as Einstellung and functional fixedness, which is how Monod and Jacob’s belief in activation delayed inhibitory control (Klahr and Simon 1999, 532–34). It also documents two opening effects: a surprise needs an expectation to violate, and analogy draws on everything stored in memory (Klahr and Simon 1999, 533, 537). Its cases locate the narrowing in knowledge held from one domain and in one representation, not in the amount known: Balmer was a geometry teacher, and the mathematicians who refit Planck’s curve in minutes did not recognize Planck’s law (Klahr and Simon 1999, 534). And the path is steered by outcomes as it goes: models given only Krebs’s starting knowledge found his reaction path, with surprise choosing each next experiment (Klahr and Simon 1999, 535). The full account, and what it changes on the graph, is on the unit page.
The quotation is not located. Its argument matches Cleland on computer models, which determine consequences under stated conditions and cannot say which conditions obtained (Cleland 2001, 989); the wording has not been checked against either Cleland paper.
The science-of-science points trace to three sources, one outside this site. Small teams disrupt and large teams develop: Wu et al. (2019), whose team-size effect Petersen and colleagues find small once reference-list growth is corrected, and reversing above eight authors (Petersen et al. 2025). The experiment-choice finding: Rzhetsky et al. (2015), an optional reading for meeting 6. That small teams last longest with a stable core is not in this site’s bibliography and has not been traced to a source. “Optimal team sizes” is not traced to a reading either. The design question, a small stable core of agents, leans on the contested part.
Simon answers discussion question 3. Klahr and Simon state the position and attribute it to Simon (1973): much empirical work is done “in the context of discovery rather than the context of verification,” and “theories cannot be tested until they have been created” (Klahr and Simon 1999, 529). On the graph that is H against K, and the room took this side: generation is search and can be done better or worse. The review gives the search argument in its own terms: with \(b\) branches at each of \(m\) moves, exhaustive search is beyond human capacity, so “effective problem solving depends in large part on processes that constrain search judiciously” (Klahr and Simon 1999, 532). The notes’ “British Museum algorithm” and “recoding the data into a more compact pattern” do not appear in the review; they are taken to come from Simon (1973) and remain unchecked against it. The nearest statement in the review defines the goal of hypothesis search as a hypothesis that accounts for the data “in a more concise or universal form” (Klahr and Simon 1999, 538).



The three questions, as the meeting left them

Can an observational study discriminate hypotheses without controlling the system? Yes, by the smoking gun, with conditions assumed rather than set, and with the risk of confirmation bias when the rival set is small.
Which research actions are not well described as a test? Pattern-finding in Simon’s sense: recoding data into a compact pattern is discovery, and whether it will hold is a later test. Exploration is the other. Klahr and Simon name both: exploratory experiments “guided by no specific hypothesis to be tested, and no clear control condition,” whose goal is “to permit phenomena to appear” (Klahr and Simon 1999, 526), and data-driven discovery, now the unit page’s sixth entry state.
Generation or warrant? Both, following Simon. The notes record no disagreement.



Open after the meeting

Whether experimental and historical science differ in kind or in degree.
Where the stable-core finding comes from, and whether it holds for agents.
Whether reading widely narrows the search. Klahr and Simon’s cases suggest the narrowing comes from reading within one domain and one representation; an agent that has read everything carries the strongest plausibility prior of all, which is the concern meeting 10 raised through Machado.
Whether the case exercise was done, each person’s own paper placed on the unit graph; the notes do not say.
Quantifying disruption, consensus, novelty, and advance, taken up in meeting 10.

title: Is there a scientific method?
text:
The agent

The unit skill, agents/skills/unit-of-inquiry/SKILL.md, runs a research agent from a trigger event along the graph, following a method people have defended. Meeting 1 wrote its first version: the node procedures and the strong-inference and trace-series methods come from these two papers. Every later meeting adds to it. The rules below are the ones these two papers force.
From Platt: no test without at least two incompatible rivals at H, or a logged reason why none could be formulated; before any experiment, the agent answers Platt’s Question, which hypothesis this outcome would disprove, and an experiment with no answer is labelled exploration (Platt 1964, 350, 352). The parallel composition, one crucial experiment shared by \(n\) units, is the skill’s first composition (Platt 1964, 347).
From Cleland: the agent records whether \(C\) was set or found; an experimental claim cannot leave V after one run; controls fixed before data may be revised after data with the reason logged, the Viking rule; rejecting an auxiliary is node P, not X, and is logged as such; a best explanation is retained with that status, never as an exclusion; “not decidable, and this would decide it” is a legal terminal state (Cleland 2001, 988; 2002, 477–80, 483–84, 492–94).
Planted flaws that test the rules: a forced single hypothesis; a test all rivals pass; a claim leaving V after one run; an exclusion that silently rejected A; a smoking gun reported as an exclusion; abstention on an answerable case.
Open: whether exclusion and best explanation are one rule with two thresholds or two rules. The room decides; the skill file records the answer.
Proposed from the September 15 discussion, not yet adopted:

At H: log how each rival was generated (analogy, known cause, a pattern in the data), so that generation strategies can be compared, as Simon’s argument requires (Klahr and Simon 1999, 529, 532). The evaluator adds a brute-force baseline, enumeration without heuristics, as the control.
At H: when prior knowledge leaves one rival, log what excluded the others before any test. A single rival with no logged reason is the ruling theory (Chamberlin 1965).
Adopted into the skill (0.2.2) and the graph (v0.3) from Klahr and Simon (1999): record the starting expectation and the plausibility order of the first rivals; keep one implausible rival until a test could favour it; and send an outcome no rival predicted along the new surprise edge from C, not to X.
At C and V: when conditions were assumed rather than set, a failed prediction goes to P with the assumption named, not to X. This is the room’s misleading disconfirmation, and the existing planted flaw, an exclusion that silently rejected A, tests it.
For meeting 13: the architecture question the room raised, a small stable core of agents, with the caveat that the team-size evidence it rests on is contested (Petersen et al. 2025).

title: Is there a scientific method?
text:
Optional extensions
On reasoning and testing. The sources behind the unit of inquiry, listed there by node. Deduction, induction, and abduction: Peirce (1992); Hanson (1958); Okasha (2016) as the one-hour introduction. The hypothesis and where it comes from: Gilbert (1886); Whewell (2014); Mill (2011). Confirmation, falsification, and the Duhem problem: Hempel (1945); Popper (2005); Duhem (1954); Quine (1951); Lakatos (1970). Eliminative induction and severity: Bacon (2004); Mayo (1996); Mayo and Spanos (2006). Inference to the best explanation: Harman (1965); Lipton (2004). Prediction against accommodation: Musgrave (1974); Douglas and Magnus (2013). Strong inference fifty years on: Davis (2006); Fudge (2014). The school version of the method and what it leaves out, from the University of Washington’s College of Education: Windschitl et al. (2008).

Chamberlin (1965): The Method of Multiple Working Hypotheses. Science (1965). Written by a geologist, and the source Platt built on. Chamberlin’s target is the single ruling hypothesis; his remedy is to hold a family of them at once. Decide whether Platt’s loop and Chamberlin’s family are the same practice.
Holmes (1987): Scientific Writing and Scientific Discovery. Isis (1987). Holmes compared laboratory notebooks with the published papers written from them and describes what the paper leaves out. The basis for standing question 5.
Gilbert (1896): The Origin of Hypotheses, Illustrated by the Discussion of a Topographic Problem. Science (1896). Grove Karl Gilbert on where a geological hypothesis comes from, worked through his own attempt to explain the Coon Butte crater: by analogy, by enumeration of the possible causes, and by the test that separates them. The geological ancestor of Platt’s method, and an account of the generative step Platt hands to Pólya.
Johnson (1933): Role of Analysis in Scientific Investigation. Geological Society of America Bulletin (1933). A geologist’s account of analysis as the method of geological investigation, with the failure modes it guards against.
Frodeman (1995): Geological reasoning: Geology as an interpretive and historical science. Geological Society of America Bulletin (1995). Geology as an interpretive and historical science, against the physics model of method. The geological statement of Cleland’s thesis, seven years earlier.
Kleinhans et al. (2005): Terra Incognita: Explanation and Reduction in Earth Science. International Studies in the Philosophy of Science (2005). What explanation and reduction mean in earth science, where the systems are open and the histories unique.
Elliott and Brook (2007): Revisiting Chamberlin: Multiple Working Hypotheses for the 21st Century. BioScience (2007). Chamberlin’s multiple working hypotheses reconsidered for present-day practice, with the model-selection tools that now implement them.
Cleland (2002): Methodological and Epistemic Differences between Historical Science and Experimental Science. Longer development of experimental/historical differences; optional elaboration of the companion.
